citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ and the chart $x=\psi_p$ on $T_0M$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection; its existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. For a
smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ write $D_t$ for the covariant derivative along
$\gamma$ of [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]] with respect to
$\nabla$ (equivalently, the pullback of the Levi–Civita connection).

1. **Metric pairing.** For smooth sections $V,W$ of the pullback bundle
   $\gamma^*TM$,
   $$\frac{d}{dt}\,g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),W(t)\bigr)=g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_tV(t),W(t)\bigr)+g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),D_tW(t)\bigr).$$
   In particular, if $D_tV=D_tW=0$ on $I$, then $g(V,W)$ is constant on $I$.

2. **Parallel transport.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise smooth curve.
   For every $v\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$ there is exactly one continuous piecewise
   smooth section $V$ of $\gamma^*TM$ with $D_tV=0$ on each smooth piece and
   $V(a)=v$; the parallel-transport map
   $P_\gamma:T_{\gamma(a)}M\to T_{\gamma(b)}M$, $v\mapsto V(b)$, is linear,
   bijective, and satisfies
   $g_{\gamma(b)}(P_\gamma v,P_\gamma w)=g_{\gamma(a)}(v,w)$ for all $v,w$.

3. **Geodesic speed and proper time.** Along a geodesic
   $\gamma:I\to M$ ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) the function
   $t\mapsto g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))$ is constant. If $\gamma$
   is nonconstant, its tangent is nowhere zero and its causal character
   (timelike, null or spacelike) is constant; a constant geodesic has zero
   tangent and is assigned none of those causal characters. If $\gamma$ is a
   **future-directed timelike geodesic** and
   $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-\lambda^2$ with $\lambda>0$, then for
   $t_0<t_1$ its proper-time increment over $[t_0,t_1]$ is
   $\lambda(t_1-t_0)/c$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]), so proper time is an
   affine parameter. In this parameter its four-velocity is
   $U=(c/\lambda)\gamma'$ and is parallel: $D_\tau U=0$. Proper time is not
   assigned to a past-directed curve by that definition; reversing the
   parameter gives a future-directed timelike geodesic with the same
   (positive) proper-time magnitude. A nonconstant null geodesic has null
   tangent and admits no proper-time parametrization.

4. **Affine reparametrizations.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a geodesic whose
   tangent is nowhere zero, and let $h:J\to I$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto
   its open image with $h'\neq0$. Then $\gamma\circ h$ is a geodesic if and
   only if $h(s)=as+b$ with constants $a\neq0$, $b$; in that case $a$ is the
   constant $h'$, and every affine parameter of this nonconstant geodesic
   arises in this way from a fixed one. If $\gamma$ is constant, then
   $\gamma\circ h$ is constant and hence geodesic for every such $h$; no
   affine restriction on $h$ follows.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ and the chart $x=\psi_p$ on $T_0M$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Under the hypotheses of Picard-Lindelof at $(t_0,x_0)$, there are $h,r,\eta>0$ such that every initial value $(s,y)$ with $|s-t_0|<\eta$ and $\|y-x_0\|_2<\eta$ has a unique solution on $[s-h,s+h]$, and all these solution graphs lie in one compact time-state cylinder.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the causal-curve class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Chart independence.** Local absolute continuity in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (a) is independent of the
chosen chart and of the smooth atlas: if one chart representative of a curve
is absolutely continuous on every compact parameter subinterval, then so is
every other one.

**(b) Velocity and smooth composition.** At every interior parameter value
$t$ at which one chart representative is differentiable, every chart
representative is differentiable, the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (b) is well defined and
independent of the chart, and the set of parameter values at which some
chart representative is differentiable has full measure in the domain. For
every smooth map $F$ of an open subset of $M$ into $M$ whose domain contains
the image of $\gamma$, the composite $F\circ\gamma$ is locally absolutely
continuous and $(F\circ\gamma)'(t)=dF_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))$ at almost
every parameter value $t$.

**(c) Piecewise $C^1$ curves.** Every piecewise $C^1$ curve (with the finite
admissible partition and one-sided endpoint convention of clause (a) of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]) is locally absolutely
continuous; a piecewise $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future causal
is a future causal curve, and if in addition its tangents are future
timelike, it is a future timelike curve.

**(d) Concatenation.** If $\gamma_1:[a,b]\to M$ and $\gamma_2:[b,c]\to M$ are
future causal curves (respectively future timelike curves) with
$\gamma_1(b)=\gamma_2(b)$, then the concatenation $\gamma:[a,c]\to M$,
$\gamma(t):=\gamma_1(t)$ for $t\le b$ and $\gamma(t):=\gamma_2(t)$ for
$t\ge b$, is a future causal (respectively future timelike) curve; the same
holds for any finite chain of such curves.

**(e) Reparametrization.** If $\varphi:J\to I$ is a strictly increasing
$C^1$ diffeomorphism of intervals with $\varphi'>0$ and $\gamma:I\to M$ is
locally absolutely continuous, then $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is locally
absolutely continuous and $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is future causal (respectively
future timelike) exactly when $\gamma$ is. Moreover $\gamma$ is
future-inextendible if and only if $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is
future-inextendible, and this equivalence holds for every strictly increasing
continuous surjection $\varphi$ of intervals, not only the $C^1$ ones.

**(f) Relations.** The relation $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is reflexive and transitive, and
$p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$ for all $p,q$; the relations $J^{\pm}$ and
$I^{\pm}$ of that definition are therefore nested, $I^{\pm}(S)\subseteq
J^{\pm}(S)$ for every $S\subseteq M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). For $w\in T_pM$ write
$h=h_n$ and $\gamma(w):=-g_p(n,w)$.

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $F : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing. Then the derivative $F'$
exists almost everywhere, is measurable, is Lebesgue integrable on $[a,b]$,
and satisfies

$$
\int_a^b F'(x)\,d\lambda(x) \le F(b)-F(a).
$$
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

derivations.claim: (Endpoint absolute continuity and extension.) Let $\gamma$ and $x$ be as in (a). By [L9] choose a Lorentz-orthonormal basis $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ at $x$, with $e_0$ future-directed. An invertible linear change of any chart centred at $x$ gives coordinates $z$ whose coordinate basis at $x$ is this basis, hence $g_{ab}(x)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. After shrinking to a coordinate ball there is $C<\infty$ such that $|v|_{\mathrm e}\le C v^0$ for every nonzero future causal vector based in that ball. To prove this, otherwise there are base points $q_n\to x$ and coordinate unit future causal vectors $v_n$ with $v_n^0<1/2$. Pass to a convergent subsequence of the unit vectors. Its unit limit $v$ satisfies $g_x(v,v)\le0$ and $g_x(v,N_x)\le0$; the latter is strict by [L9], so $v$ is future causal. Thus $v^0>0$ and $|v_s|\le v^0$ in the chosen orthonormal basis, giving $v^0\ge1/\sqrt2$, a contradiction. The coordinate $z^0$ is therefore strictly increasing on future causal curves in this ball, and supplies the local strict temporal coordinate. Choose $a<b$ so the tail of $\gamma$ stays in this chart, write $y=z\circ\gamma$, and extend $y(b)=z(x)$. Put $\tau=y^0$; on each compact subinterval of $[a,b)$, the AC chain rule and FTC give $\tau'>0$ and $|y'|_{\mathrm e}\le C\tau'$ almost everywhere and make $\tau$ strictly increasing. Its continuous endpoint extension is bounded and nondecreasing on $[a,b]$, so [L10] gives $\tau'\in L^1[a,b]$. Consequently each component of $y'$ is integrable on $[a,b]$. For $t<b$ the local FTC gives $y(t)=y(a)+\int_a^t y'$ componentwise; letting $t\uparrow b$ gives the same identity at $b$, since the integral of an L1 function is continuous and $y(t)\to y(b)$. Thus the endpoint extension of $y$ is AC on $[a,b]$ by [L10], and retains its original nonzero future causal velocity almost everywhere. Choose a future timelike $w\in T_xM$; [L4] supplies a short geodesic $\beta(s)=\exp_x(sw)$ with $\beta(0)=x$, whose tangents are future timelike by [L3]. Concatenate the now AC closed tail with $\beta$ by [L7] and leave the earlier part of $\gamma$ unchanged. This defines the required future causal $\tilde\gamma$ on $I\cup[b,b+\varepsilon)$ and proves (a). The past case reverses time.

(Set-up for the maximal geodesic.) Suppose, for contradiction, that $\gamma:=\gamma_{p,v}$ with $v
e0$ converges to some $x\in M$ at one of its ends. Treat the upper end $b:=\sup I_{p,v}$, the past case being the time reverse of the same argument. Choose a chart $(U,y)$ around $x$ with $y(x)=0$; by convergence there is $t_1<b$ with $\gamma([t_1,b))\subseteq K$ for a compact $K\subseteq U$. Put $K'=y(K)$, a compact subset of the open coordinate domain $y(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$. Write $y(t):=y(\gamma(t))$ and $w(t):=y'(t)$ for $t\in[t_1,b)$; the curve is smooth and $w(t)
e0$ for all $t$, by uniqueness, including when $v$ is null: if $\gamma'(t_*)=0$ at any interior parameter, its geodesic initial data at $t_*$ agree with the constant geodesic at $\gamma(t_*)$. Local uniqueness of the chart geodesic ODE [L2], [L6] makes them agree near $t_*$. The agreement set is closed and locally open in the connected geodesic interval, so they agree throughout, contradicting $v
e0$. Put $ho(t):=|w(t)|_{\mathrm e}>0$, $u(t):=w(t)/ho(t)\in S^3$, and $\sigma(t):=\int_{t_1}^tho$, a strictly increasing $C^1$ function with $\sigma'=ho>0$. Let $\sigma_\infty:=\lim_{t	o b}\sigma(t)\in(0,\infty]$ and let $t(\sigma)$ be the inverse of $\sigma$ on $[0,\sigma_\infty)$. By [L2], $w'=-\Gamma(y)(w,w)$ componentwise.

(A maximal solution whose graph stays in a compact set has no finite endpoint.) Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:O\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $z:[0,\tau_\infty)\to O$ be a maximal solution of $z'=F(z)$ whose graph is contained in a compact set $K\subseteq O$. If $\tau_\infty<\infty$, then $z$ extends to a solution on a strictly larger interval: indeed, by compactness of $K$ and [L5], finitely many cylinders cover $K$ and there is a common $h>0$ such that every initial condition in $K$ admits a solution on an interval of length $h$ contained in $O$; decreasing $h$ if necessary so that $h<\tau_\infty$, and starting from $z(\tau_\infty-h/2)$ and invoking uniqueness [L6] extends $z$ past $\tau_\infty$, contradicting maximality. Hence $\tau_\infty=\infty$.

(The normalized equations in both parameters.) Put $Q(y,u):=\Gamma(y)(u,u)$ and $a(y,u):=\langle u,Q(y,u)\rangle_{\mathrm e}$. In the affine parameter $t$, differentiating $\rho=|w|_{\mathrm e}$ and $u=w/\rho$ gives $\frac{d\rho}{dt}=-\rho^2a(y,u)$ and $\frac{du}{dt}=-\rho P_uQ(y,u)$, where for unit $u$, $P_u=I-u\otimes u$ is the Euclidean orthogonal projection onto $u^\perp$. Since $d\sigma/dt=\rho$, in the parameter $\sigma$ the fields $Y(\sigma)=y(t(\sigma))$, $U(\sigma)=u(t(\sigma))$, and $r(\sigma)=\rho(t(\sigma))$ satisfy $\frac{dY}{d\sigma}=U$, $\frac{dU}{d\sigma}=-P_UQ(Y,U)$, and $\frac{dr}{d\sigma}=-r a(Y,U)$. For ODE continuation extend $P_U$ off the unit sphere by $I-U\otimes U$; this defines a smooth field on the open coordinate domain times $\mathbb R^4$. The unit sphere is invariant: $q=|U|_{\mathrm e}^2-1$ satisfies $q'=2a(Y,U)q$, so the zero initial value forces $q=0$. Thus the normalized solution remains unit-speed in $\sigma$.

(Finite normalized length forces a finite affine end and extension.) Suppose $\sigma_\infty<\infty$. On the original normalized interval $(Y,U)$ lies in the compact set $y(K)\times S^3$ inside the coordinate ODE domain. Its maximal ODE extension from the initial data therefore passes beyond $\sigma_\infty$ by step 1.3 and uniqueness [L6]. Choose $\delta>0$ so this extension on $[0,\sigma_\infty+\delta]$ still has coordinate values in the chart; by the sphere invariance of step 2.1 its direction remains unit. The continuous coefficient $a(Y,U)$ is bounded there, by $C$ say. Its speed is $r(\sigma)=\rho(t_1)\exp(-\int_0^\sigma a(Y,U)\,ds)$, so $0<\rho(t_1)e^{-C(\sigma_\infty+\delta)}\le r(\sigma)\le\rho(t_1)e^{C(\sigma_\infty+\delta)}<\infty$. In particular, on the original interval $t(\sigma)=t_1+\int_0^\sigma r(s)^{-1}\,ds$ has a finite limit $t_1+\int_0^{\sigma_\infty}r^{-1}$; since this is the inverse of $\sigma(t)$, that limit equals $b$, so this case explicitly excludes $b=+\infty$. On the extended interval this strictly increasing smooth affine-time reconstruction attains values greater than $b$. Its inverse gives $dy/dt=rU$ and $d(rU)/dt=r\,d(rU)/d\sigma=-r^2Q(Y,U)$ by step 2.1, hence the coordinate geodesic equation [L2]. The reconstructed curve agrees with $\gamma$ on the old tail by uniqueness, glues with its earlier part, and extends the affine geodesic past $b$. This contradicts maximality [L1].

(Second case: infinite $\sigma_\infty$.) Suppose $\sigma_\infty=\infty$. Then $t(\sigma)\to b$ as $\sigma\to\infty$, and by convergence of $\gamma$ one has $Y(\sigma)=y(t(\sigma))\to0$ in the chart. By step 2.1, $|U'|_{\mathrm e}=|P_U\Gamma(Y)(U,U)|_{\mathrm e}\le C$ on the compact set $K'\times S^3$. Let $\sigma>0$ and $L>0$; the mean value bound [L8] gives $\left|U(\sigma)-\frac1L\int_\sigma^{\sigma+L}U\right|_{\mathrm e}\le\frac{CL}{2}$, while $\left|\frac1L\int_\sigma^{\sigma+L}U\right|_{\mathrm e}=\frac1L|Y(\sigma+L)-Y(\sigma)|_{\mathrm e}\le\frac1L\bigl(|Y(\sigma+L)|_{\mathrm e}+|Y(\sigma)|_{\mathrm e}\bigr)$. Choose $L$ with $CL<1$ and then $\sigma$ so large that the last expression is less than $\frac12$; then $|U(\sigma)|_{\mathrm e}<\frac12+\frac12=1$, contradicting $|U|_{\mathrm e}=1$. Hence $\sigma_\infty=\infty$ is impossible.

(Conclusions.) Steps 3.1 and 3.2 show that a maximal geodesic with $v\ne0$ cannot converge at either end, which is (b); the past end is the time reverse of the same argument. For (c), let $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to M$ be future causal. Choose a future timelike $w_1\in T_{\gamma(t_0)}M$ and a future timelike $w_2\in T_{\gamma(t_1)}M$. By [L1] there are maximal geodesics $\gamma_1:=\gamma_{\gamma(t_0),w_1}$ and $\gamma_2:=\gamma_{\gamma(t_1),w_2}$; both are future-directed and smooth on their domains by [L3], and they contain $\gamma(t_0)$ at parameter $0$ and $\gamma(t_1)$ at parameter $0$ respectively. Concatenating the restriction of $\gamma_1$ to $(\inf I_1,0]$, the curve $\gamma$ (after shifting the parameter), and the restriction of $\gamma_2$ to $[0,\sup I_2)$ gives a future causal curve $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ by [L7], where $J$ is the corresponding interval, and there is a strictly increasing affine identification of $[t_0,t_1]$ with a subinterval of $J$ carrying $\gamma$ to $\hat\gamma$. By (b) the maximal geodesics do not converge at their outer ends, so the two outer ends of $\hat\gamma$ have no limits, at finite or infinite endpoints alike; this is exactly inextendibility in [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d). If $p\ne q$ and $p\le q$, a future causal curve from $p$ to $q$ exists by the definition of $\le$, and the construction applies to it; the past case is the time reverse. This proves (c).

(Cauchy sets are acausal.) Let $S$ be a Cauchy set in the sense of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c). Suppose $p,q\in S$ are distinct and $p\le q$. Choose a future causal curve $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to M$ with $\gamma(t_0)=p$ and $\gamma(t_1)=q$, and let $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ and the affine identification $\rho$ be as in (c). Then $\hat\gamma$ is an inextendible causal curve and $\rho(t_0)\ne\rho(t_1)$, since $\rho$ is strictly increasing and $t_0<t_1$ while $\hat\gamma(\rho(t_0))=p\ne q=\hat\gamma(\rho(t_1))$; thus the parameter set $\hat\gamma^{-1}[S]$ contains the two distinct elements $\rho(t_0)$ and $\rho(t_1)$, contradicting the defining property of a Cauchy set. The relation $q\le p$ is excluded symmetrically by the past version of (c). Hence no two distinct points of $S$ are causally related, that is, $S$ is acausal; this is (d) and completes the proof.

citations.quote:
If a Lie group $G$ acts smoothly, freely, and properly on a smooth manifold
$M$, then the orbit space $M/G$ with its quotient topology is a Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold of dimension
$\dim M-\dim G$. It has a unique smooth structure for which the quotient map
$q:M\to M/G$ is a smooth surjective submersion.

A smooth action of a Lie group $G$ on a manifold $M$ is **free** if
$G_x=\{e\}$ for every $x\in M$.

It is **proper** if its action-graph map

$$\Theta:G\times M\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Theta(g,x)=(g\cdot x,x),$$

is proper: $\Theta^{-1}(K)$ is compact for every compact
$K\subseteq M\times M$. The reversed coordinate convention
$(x,g\cdot x)$ is equivalent by the factor-swap homeomorphism. Freeness and
properness are independent conditions; neither is encoded by the other.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

derivations.claim: (The quotient and local diffeomorphism property.) By [L1] and [L2], $M$ is a Hausdorff second-countable smooth four-manifold and $q$ is a smooth surjective submersion. Since $\dim M=\dim\hat M$, the differential $dq_p:T_p\hat M\to T_{q(p)}M$ is a linear isomorphism for every $p$: it is onto by the submersion property and the spaces have the same finite dimension. By [L3] every point of $\hat M$ has an open neighborhood $\hat U$ such that $q|_{\hat U}:\hat U\to q(\hat U)$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open set; in particular there are smooth local sections $s:V\to\hat M$ with $q\circ s=\operatorname{id}_V$ over open sets $V\subseteq M$ covering $M$. This proves (a).

(The metric: well-definedness.) For $r\in M$ and $v,w\in T_rM$ choose $p\in q^{-1}(r)$ and the unique $\hat V,\hat W\in T_p\hat M$ with $dq_p\hat V=v$, $dq_p\hat W=w$, and set $g_r(v,w):=\hat g_p(\hat V,\hat W)$. To see that this is independent of the choice of $p$: if $p'=\gamma\cdot p$, then by [L4] and the injectivity of $dq_{p'}$ the unique preimage of $v$ at $p'$ is $d\gamma_p\hat V$, and similarly for $w$, so the defining cocycle identity of the statement gives $\hat g_{p'}(d\gamma_p\hat V,d\gamma_p\hat W)=\hat g_p(\hat V,\hat W)$. The assignment is symmetric and bilinear in $(v,w)$ at each $r$ because $\hat g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate with signature $(-,+,+,+)$ because $dq_p$ is a linear isomorphism and $\hat g_p$ is nondegenerate of that signature ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

(Smoothness and uniqueness.) Let $s:V\to\hat M$ be a smooth local section of $q$ as in step 1.1. For $r\in V$ and $v,w\in T_rM$ one has $dq_{s(r)}\circ ds_r=\operatorname{id}_{T_rM}$, so $g_r(v,w)=\hat g_{s(r)}(ds_rv,ds_rw)$, that is, $g|_V=s^*\hat g$. Both $s$ and $\hat g$ are smooth, so the components of $g$ in any chart contained in $V$ are smooth; since the open sets $V$ cover $M$, $g$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). If $g'$ were another smooth metric with $q^*g'=\hat g$, then for every $r$, $v,w$ and choice of $p$, $\hat V,\hat W$ as in step 2.1 one would have $g'_r(v,w)=\hat g_p(\hat V,\hat W)=g_r(v,w)$, so $g'=g$. This proves (b).

(The time orientation.) Let $\hat N$ be $\Gamma$-invariant with $\hat g(\hat N,\hat N)<0$. For $p'=\gamma\cdot p$ the invariance gives $d\gamma_p\hat N_p=\hat N_{p'}$, so $dq_{p'}\hat N_{p'}=dq_{p'}(d\gamma_p\hat N_p)=dq_p\hat N_p$ by [L4]; hence $N_{q(p)}:=dq_p\hat N_p$ is well defined on $M$, and it is smooth because over a local section $s$ it equals $dq_{s(r)}\hat N_{s(r)}=ds_r^{-1}\hat N_{s(r)}$, a smooth expression. Moreover $g(N,N)_{q(p)}=\hat g_p(\hat N_p,\hat N_p)<0$ by the defining formula of step 2.1; so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,g)$ in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c).
(Conclusion.) Part (a) is step 1.1, part (b) is steps 2.1 and 3.1, and part (c) is step 3.2; this completes the proof.

risk_review.notes: Read all five proof steps and all eight direct supplier definitions/statements. Free proper smooth Lie-group quotient gives Hausdorff second-countable quotient and dimension difference; discreteness gives equal dimension, submersion then invertible differential. Metric and invariant timelike field are representative-independent by q∘γ=q and isometry. Local inverse sections give smoothness and uniqueness. No global representative choice is made; inherited AC_omega is retained through smooth-vector-field definition. Empty manifold is vacuous; zero vector cannot serve as time orientation. No causal conclusion is asserted.

step 5.1 establishes vanishing of sigma and omega exactly at the zero tensor; the factor 1/3 is the inverse rest-space dimension.
step 2.1 proves h is positive definite on the three-dimensional rest space and identifies h^{ab} as a projection, not an inverse of a degenerate form.

citations.quote:
Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open subset.

**(a) Geodesic congruence.** A **smooth future unit timelike geodesic
congruence** on $U$ is an observer congruence $n$ on $U$
([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]],
[[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so that
$g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,N)<0$ on $U$, which in addition is geodesic:
$$\nabla_nn=0\qquad\text{on }U .$$
Thus each observer curve of the congruence is an affinely parametrized
geodesic ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) and its flow parameter is
affine; by [[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]] the tangent is
future unit timelike at every parameter value.

**(b) Observer curves.** By [[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]]
each $q\in U$ lies on a unique maximal integral curve
$\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$; these are the **observer
curves** or **flow lines** of the congruence, and their parameter $s$ is the
**affine parameter** of the geodesic. The mathematical proper-time function
$\tau$ of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]], normalized by
$\tau(0)=0$, satisfies
$$\tau(s_2)-\tau(s_1)=\frac{1}{c}\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\sqrt{-g(n,n)}\,ds=\frac{s_2-s_1}{c}\qquad(s_1<s_2,\ s_1,s_2\in I_q).$$
Thus $\tau(s)=s/c$ with this normalization. This is the metric-defined
mathematical proper-time parameter, not a clock reading; the ideal-clock
interpretation is a separate physical assumption.

**(c) Kinematic quantities.** On $U$ define the smooth covariant $2$-tensor
field
$$B_{ab}:=\nabla_bn_a,\qquad n_a:=g_{ab}n^b ,$$
the **rest-space metric field**
$$h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+n_an_b,$$
with index-raised field $h^{ab}:=g^{ab}+n^an^b$ built from the inverse metric
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]), and:
$$\theta:=g^{ab}B_{ab},\qquad \sigma_{ab}:=B_{(ab)}-\tfrac13\theta\,h_{ab},\qquad \omega_{ab}:=B_{[ab]},$$
the **expansion**, **shear** and **vorticity** of the congruence, where
$B_{(ab)}=\tfrac12(B_{ab}+B_{ba})$ and $B_{[ab]}=\tfrac12(B_{ab}-B_{ba})$.
The three fields $\theta$, $\sigma$, $\omega$ and the tensor $B$ are smooth
in every chart ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), because
components of $\nabla n$, $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are smooth.

**(d) Scope.** The definition asserts no dynamical equation, no sign of
$\theta$ and no physical interpretation. In particular the identities making
$\sigma$ and $\omega$ rest-space tensors, their tracelessness and
antisymmetry, and the decomposition $B=\tfrac13\theta h+\sigma+\omega$ are
proved in [[lem-gr-kinematic-decomposition-identities]], not assumed here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty
open subset, carrying the restricted smooth structure of
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]].

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field
$n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that
$n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly,

$$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$

Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing. A single observer
at a point is therefore not a congruence, and a congruence is not an ordered
basis or frame of $T_qM$.

**(b) Observer curves.** Because $n$ is a smooth vector field on $U$, the
theorem on maximal integral curves
([[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]],
[[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]]) assigns to every $q\in U$ a unique
maximal integral curve $\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$,
defined on an open interval $I_q\subseteq\mathbb R$. We call these curves the
**observers** (or **observer curves**) of the congruence. Each observer is
regular: $\gamma_q'(s)=n_{\gamma_q(s)}$ and $\lVert n\rVert_g=1$ at every
parameter value, so the tangent vector is unit timelike and future-directed at
every parameter value. Completeness of the maximal intervals $I_q$, and global
product or foliation structure of $U$, are not asserted. The parameter $s$ is
the flow parameter of $n$; it is not identified with any clock reading here.

**(c) Adapted charts.** An **$n$-adapted chart** is a smooth chart
$(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U'\to\mathbb R^4$ of $M$ whose domain $U'$ is a nonempty
open subset of $U$ and whose **spatial coordinates** $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant
along every integral curve of $n$ contained in $U'$; equivalently, for every
$q\in U'$ the observer curve $\gamma_q$ satisfies
$u^i(\gamma_q(s))=u^i(q)$ for all $s$ with $\gamma_q(s)\in U'$ and
$i=1,2,3$. No global adapted chart, and no adapted chart on all of $U$, is
asserted by this definition; one exists near every point of $U$ by the
existence corollary proved on this page.

**(d) Scope.** A congruence is a field of observer directions on an open set; it
is not a chart, not a tetrad field, and not a family of parametrized
worldlines with specified domains. The physical reading of its observer curves
as ideal-clock worldlines, and the identification of the flow parameter with a
measurable time, belong to the physical postulates of the framework and are not
asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.
