Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$R$, $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ be as in
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then the following
identities hold for all indices $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and at every point of
every smooth chart:

**(a) Skew-symmetries.** $R_{abcd}=-R_{bacd}$ and $R_{abcd}=-R_{abdc}$.
Equivalently, for smooth vector fields,
$$g\bigl(R(X,Y)Z,W\bigr)=-g\bigl(R(X,Y)W,Z\bigr) \quad\text{and}\quad g\bigl(R(X,Y)Z,W\bigr)=-g\bigl(R(Y,X)Z,W\bigr).$$

**(b) Exchange of the index pairs.** $R_{abcd}=R_{cdab}$, equivalently
$g\bigl(R(X,Y)Z,W\bigr)=g\bigl(R(Z,W)X,Y\bigr)$.

**(c) First Bianchi identity.** $R_{a[bcd]}=0$, that is,
$$R_{abcd}+R_{acdb}+R_{adbc}=0 .$$

**(d) Ricci symmetry.** $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ba}$;
consequently the Einstein tensor is symmetric, $G_{ab}=G_{ba}$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), whose geodesics
and exponential map are those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]].

**(a) Point-normal charts.** For every $p\in M$ there is a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$ such that, in the components of this chart,

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0,\qquad \partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0,\qquad g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}.$$

The construction starts from any chart around $p$ and is finite: no frame field
on $U$ and no global trivialization of $TM$ is used.

**(b) Exponential charts.** For every $p\in M$ and every $g_p$-orthonormal
basis $e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$ there is a star-shaped open neighborhood
$W\subseteq T_pM$ of $0$ on which $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open
$U_p\ni p$, and the chart

$$u:=\psi\circ\exp_p^{-1}:U_p\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,$$

where $\psi:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ is the coordinate isomorphism of the basis,
satisfies $u(p)=0$ and the same three normal-form identities at $p$ as in (a).
Moreover every geodesic through $p$ has, in the chart $u$, the form
$u(\gamma(t))=(t-t_0)\,k$ for a constant $k\in\mathbb R^4$ whenever
$\gamma(t_0)=p$, $k=\psi(\gamma'(t_0))$, and
$(t-t_0)\gamma'(t_0)\in W$. Thus the portion represented by its radial initial
vector in $W$ is a straight coordinate ray through the origin. This claim is
not made for a later portion of a geodesic that may return to $U_p$ after its
radial initial vector has left $W$. No assertion is made about the second
derivatives of the metric at $p$: the construction is first order and does not
make a neighborhood of $p$ isometric to Minkowski space.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open subset.

**(a) Geodesic congruence.** A **smooth future unit timelike geodesic
congruence** on $U$ is an observer congruence $n$ on $U$
([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]],
[[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so that
$g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,N)<0$ on $U$, which in addition is geodesic:
$$\nabla_nn=0\qquad\text{on }U .$$
Thus each observer curve of the congruence is an affinely parametrized
geodesic ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) and its flow parameter is
affine; by [[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]] the tangent is
future unit timelike at every parameter value.

**(b) Observer curves.** By [[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]]
each $q\in U$ lies on a unique maximal integral curve
$\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$; these are the **observer
curves** or **flow lines** of the congruence, and their parameter $s$ is the
**affine parameter** of the geodesic. The mathematical proper-time function
$\tau$ of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]], normalized by
$\tau(0)=0$, satisfies
$$\tau(s_2)-\tau(s_1)=\frac{1}{c}\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\sqrt{-g(n,n)}\,ds=\frac{s_2-s_1}{c}\qquad(s_1<s_2,\ s_1,s_2\in I_q).$$
Thus $\tau(s)=s/c$ with this normalization. This is the metric-defined
mathematical proper-time parameter, not a clock reading; the ideal-clock
interpretation is a separate physical assumption.

**(c) Kinematic quantities.** On $U$ define the smooth covariant $2$-tensor
field
$$B_{ab}:=\nabla_bn_a,\qquad n_a:=g_{ab}n^b ,$$
the **rest-space metric field**
$$h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+n_an_b,$$
with index-raised field $h^{ab}:=g^{ab}+n^an^b$ built from the inverse metric
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]), and:
$$\theta:=g^{ab}B_{ab},\qquad \sigma_{ab}:=B_{(ab)}-\tfrac13\theta\,h_{ab},\qquad \omega_{ab}:=B_{[ab]},$$
the **expansion**, **shear** and **vorticity** of the congruence, where
$B_{(ab)}=\tfrac12(B_{ab}+B_{ba})$ and $B_{[ab]}=\tfrac12(B_{ab}-B_{ba})$.
The three fields $\theta$, $\sigma$, $\omega$ and the tensor $B$ are smooth
in every chart ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), because
components of $\nabla n$, $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are smooth.

**(d) Scope.** The definition asserts no dynamical equation, no sign of
$\theta$ and no physical interpretation. In particular the identities making
$\sigma$ and $\omega$ rest-space tensors, their tracelessness and
antisymmetry, and the decomposition $B=\tfrac13\theta h+\sigma+\omega$ are
proved in [[lem-gr-kinematic-decomposition-identities]], not assumed here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty
open subset, carrying the restricted smooth structure of
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]].

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field
$n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that
$n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly,

$$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$

Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing. A single observer
at a point is therefore not a congruence, and a congruence is not an ordered
basis or frame of $T_qM$.

**(b) Observer curves.** Because $n$ is a smooth vector field on $U$, the
theorem on maximal integral curves
([[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]],
[[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]]) assigns to every $q\in U$ a unique
maximal integral curve $\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$,
defined on an open interval $I_q\subseteq\mathbb R$. We call these curves the
**observers** (or **observer curves**) of the congruence. Each observer is
regular: $\gamma_q'(s)=n_{\gamma_q(s)}$ and $\lVert n\rVert_g=1$ at every
parameter value, so the tangent vector is unit timelike and future-directed at
every parameter value. Completeness of the maximal intervals $I_q$, and global
product or foliation structure of $U$, are not asserted. The parameter $s$ is
the flow parameter of $n$; it is not identified with any clock reading here.

**(c) Adapted charts.** An **$n$-adapted chart** is a smooth chart
$(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U'\to\mathbb R^4$ of $M$ whose domain $U'$ is a nonempty
open subset of $U$ and whose **spatial coordinates** $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant
along every integral curve of $n$ contained in $U'$; equivalently, for every
$q\in U'$ the observer curve $\gamma_q$ satisfies
$u^i(\gamma_q(s))=u^i(q)$ for all $s$ with $\gamma_q(s)\in U'$ and
$i=1,2,3$. No global adapted chart, and no adapted chart on all of $U$, is
asserted by this definition; one exists near every point of $U$ by the
existence corollary proved on this page.

**(d) Scope.** A congruence is a field of observer directions on an open set; it
is not a chart, not a tetrad field, and not a family of parametrized
worldlines with specified domains. The physical reading of its observer curves
as ideal-clock worldlines, and the identification of the flow parameter with a
measurable time, belong to the physical postulates of the framework and are not
asserted here.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and curvature $R$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). For a smooth vector field
$Z$ let $A$ be the smooth $(1,1)$-tensor field $A^a{}_b:=\nabla_bZ^a$ and
let $B:=\nabla A$ be its covariant derivative, $B^a{}_{bc}:=\nabla_bA^a{}_c$
([[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]] for the
extension of $\nabla$ to tensor fields).

**(a)** For all smooth vector fields $Z$ and all indices,
$$B^a{}_{bc}-B^a{}_{cb}=R^a{}_{dbc}Z^d .$$

**(b)** Contracting the first index with the second lower index,
$$B^a{}_{ab}-B^a{}_{ba}=\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}Z^d .$$

**(c)** For all smooth vector fields $V,Z$,
$$V^c\nabla_c(\nabla_aZ^a)=\nabla_a\bigl(V^c\nabla_cZ^a\bigr) -(\nabla_aV^c)(\nabla_cZ^a)-\operatorname{Ric}_{cd}V^cZ^d ,$$
where $\nabla_aW^a$ denotes the divergence of a vector field and
$\nabla_a(V^c\nabla_cZ^a)$ is the divergence of the vector field
$W^a:=V^c\nabla_cZ^a$.

Let $n$ be a geodesic congruence with kinematic quantities $B$, $\theta$,
$\sigma$, $\omega$ and $h$ on $U$ as in
[[def-gr-geodesic-congruence-and-kinematics]], and write
$h^{ab}:=g^{ab}+n^an^b$. Then, everywhere on $U$:

**(a)** $n^aB_{ab}=0$ and $B_{ab}n^b=0$; hence $B$ takes values in the
rest-space bundle $n^{\perp}$ in both slots
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]).

**(b)** $h_{ab}n^b=0$, the restriction of $h$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
definite, $h^{ab}h_{bc}=\delta^a_c+n^an_c$, and $h_{ab}h^{ba}=3$.

**(c)** $\sigma_{ab}$ is symmetric and $h^{ab}\sigma_{ab}=0$;
$\omega_{ab}$ is antisymmetric; and
$B_{ab}=\tfrac13\theta\,h_{ab}+\sigma_{ab}+\omega_{ab}$.

**(d)** $B_{ab}B^{ba}=\tfrac13\theta^2+\sigma_{ab}\sigma^{ab}-\omega_{ab}\omega^{ab}$,
where all indices are raised with $g$; moreover
$\sigma_{ab}\sigma^{ab}\ge0$ and $\omega_{ab}\omega^{ab}\ge0$, the first
vanishing exactly when $\sigma=0$ and the second exactly when $\omega=0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open subset.

**(a) Geodesic congruence.** A **smooth future unit timelike geodesic
congruence** on $U$ is an observer congruence $n$ on $U$
([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]],
[[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so that
$g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,N)<0$ on $U$, which in addition is geodesic:
$$\nabla_nn=0\qquad\text{on }U .$$
Thus each observer curve of the congruence is an affinely parametrized
geodesic ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) and its flow parameter is
affine; by [[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]] the tangent is
future unit timelike at every parameter value.

**(b) Observer curves.** By [[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]]
each $q\in U$ lies on a unique maximal integral curve
$\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$; these are the **observer
curves** or **flow lines** of the congruence, and their parameter $s$ is the
**affine parameter** of the geodesic. The mathematical proper-time function
$\tau$ of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]], normalized by
$\tau(0)=0$, satisfies
$$\tau(s_2)-\tau(s_1)=\frac{1}{c}\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\sqrt{-g(n,n)}\,ds=\frac{s_2-s_1}{c}\qquad(s_1<s_2,\ s_1,s_2\in I_q).$$
Thus $\tau(s)=s/c$ with this normalization. This is the metric-defined
mathematical proper-time parameter, not a clock reading; the ideal-clock
interpretation is a separate physical assumption.

**(c) Kinematic quantities.** On $U$ define the smooth covariant $2$-tensor
field
$$B_{ab}:=\nabla_bn_a,\qquad n_a:=g_{ab}n^b ,$$
the **rest-space metric field**
$$h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+n_an_b,$$
with index-raised field $h^{ab}:=g^{ab}+n^an^b$ built from the inverse metric
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]), and:
$$\theta:=g^{ab}B_{ab},\qquad \sigma_{ab}:=B_{(ab)}-\tfrac13\theta\,h_{ab},\qquad \omega_{ab}:=B_{[ab]},$$
the **expansion**, **shear** and **vorticity** of the congruence, where
$B_{(ab)}=\tfrac12(B_{ab}+B_{ba})$ and $B_{[ab]}=\tfrac12(B_{ab}-B_{ba})$.
The three fields $\theta$, $\sigma$, $\omega$ and the tensor $B$ are smooth
in every chart ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), because
components of $\nabla n$, $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are smooth.

**(d) Scope.** The definition asserts no dynamical equation, no sign of
$\theta$ and no physical interpretation. In particular the identities making
$\sigma$ and $\omega$ rest-space tensors, their tracelessness and
antisymmetry, and the decomposition $B=\tfrac13\theta h+\sigma+\omega$ are
proved in [[lem-gr-kinematic-decomposition-identities]], not assumed here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim:
(Reduction of the curvature and quadratic terms.) Apply [L3] with $V=Z=n$: the first term on the right vanishes by [L5], so $$n^c
abla_c(
abla_an^a)=-(
abla_an^c)(
abla_cn^a)-\operatorname{Ric}_{cd}n^cn^d .$$ The quadratic term is $B_{ab}B^{ba}$: since $B_{ab}=
abla_bn_a$, raising gives $
abla_an^c=g^{cb}B_{ba}$ and $
abla_cn^a=g^{ad}B_{dc}$, so $(
abla_an^c)(
abla_cn^a)=B_{ab}B^{ba}$. By [L1] and [L2], the left side is $ rac{d}{ds} igl(	heta(\gamma(s)) igr)$, and by [L4] the quadratic term equals $	frac13	heta^2+\sigma_{ab}\sigma^{ab}-\omega_{ab}\omega^{ab}$. Substituting, with all fields evaluated at $\gamma(s)$, gives exactly the displayed equation of (a).

(Differential inequality and integration.) Assume now $\omega=0$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}n^an^b\ge0$ on $U$, and define $y(s):=-\theta(\gamma(s))$ for $s\in I_q$. By (a), $y'(s)=\tfrac13\theta^2+\sigma_{ab}\sigma^{ab}+\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}n^an^b\ge\tfrac13y(s)^2\ge0$, where nonnegativity of $\sigma_{ab}\sigma^{ab}$ and of the Ricci term was used. At $s_0$ one has $y(s_0)=-\theta_0>0$; hence, as long as $s>s_0$ and $y>0$, $\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(1/y(s)\bigr)=-\frac{y'(s)}{y(s)^2}\le-\frac13$. Integrating from $s_0$ to $s$ by [L6] gives $\frac{1}{y(s)}\le\frac{1}{y(s_0)}-\frac{s-s_0}{3}$.

(Positivity and the bound.) Let $J$ be the connected component of $\{s\in I_q:s\ge s_0,\ y(s)>0\}$ containing $s_0$; it contains a right-neighborhood of $s_0$. On $J$, step 2.1 gives $y'(s)\ge y(s)^2/3>0$, so $y$ is increasing and $y(s)\ge y(s_0)>0$. Thus $J$ cannot have a right endpoint strictly inside $I_q$: continuity there gives a positive limiting value, allowing $J$ to continue. Therefore $y>0$ on $[s_0,\sup I_q)$, and the reciprocal estimate of step 2.1 holds for every $s>s_0$ in $I_q$. Since $1/y(s)>0$, that estimate gives $s<s_0+3/(-\theta_0)$ for every such $s$, hence $\sup I_q\le s_0+3/(-\theta_0)$. The stated continuation conclusion follows for any continuation on which the smooth congruence and both sign hypotheses persist; this proves (b) and completes the proof.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the causal-curve class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Chart independence.** Local absolute continuity in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (a) is independent of the
chosen chart and of the smooth atlas: if one chart representative of a curve
is absolutely continuous on every compact parameter subinterval, then so is
every other one.

**(b) Velocity and smooth composition.** At every interior parameter value
$t$ at which one chart representative is differentiable, every chart
representative is differentiable, the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (b) is well defined and
independent of the chart, and the set of parameter values at which some
chart representative is differentiable has full measure in the domain. For
every smooth map $F$ of an open subset of $M$ into $M$ whose domain contains
the image of $\gamma$, the composite $F\circ\gamma$ is locally absolutely
continuous and $(F\circ\gamma)'(t)=dF_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))$ at almost
every parameter value $t$.

**(c) Piecewise $C^1$ curves.** Every piecewise $C^1$ curve (with the finite
admissible partition and one-sided endpoint convention of clause (a) of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]) is locally absolutely
continuous; a piecewise $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future causal
is a future causal curve, and if in addition its tangents are future
timelike, it is a future timelike curve.

**(d) Concatenation.** If $\gamma_1:[a,b]\to M$ and $\gamma_2:[b,c]\to M$ are
future causal curves (respectively future timelike curves) with
$\gamma_1(b)=\gamma_2(b)$, then the concatenation $\gamma:[a,c]\to M$,
$\gamma(t):=\gamma_1(t)$ for $t\le b$ and $\gamma(t):=\gamma_2(t)$ for
$t\ge b$, is a future causal (respectively future timelike) curve; the same
holds for any finite chain of such curves.

**(e) Reparametrization.** If $\varphi:J\to I$ is a strictly increasing
$C^1$ diffeomorphism of intervals with $\varphi'>0$ and $\gamma:I\to M$ is
locally absolutely continuous, then $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is locally
absolutely continuous and $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is future causal (respectively
future timelike) exactly when $\gamma$ is. Moreover $\gamma$ is
future-inextendible if and only if $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is
future-inextendible, and this equivalence holds for every strictly increasing
continuous surjection $\varphi$ of intervals, not only the $C^1$ ones.

**(f) Relations.** The relation $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is reflexive and transitive, and
$p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$ for all $p,q$; the relations $J^{\pm}$ and
$I^{\pm}$ of that definition are therefore nested, $I^{\pm}(S)\subseteq
J^{\pm}(S)$ for every $S\subseteq M$.

Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], let $y$ be an inertial
chart, let $p\in M$, and let $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$v=v^0\partial_0+\dots+v^3\partial_3$ in the chart
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]). Write
$v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and $|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

**(a)** For every nonzero $v\in T_pM$: $v$ is future timelike iff
$v^0>|v_s|$, and past timelike iff $v^0<-|v_s|$; $v$ is future null iff
$0<v^0=|v_s|$, and past null iff $0<-v^0=|v_s|$; $v$ is future causal iff
$v^0\ge|v_s|$, past causal iff $v^0\le-|v_s|$, and causal iff
$|v^0|\ge|v_s|$; and every nonzero future causal $v$ satisfies $v^0>0$.

**(b)** $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)=\{v\in T_pM:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; the future-directed
causal vectors are exactly $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}
=\{v\neq0:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$.

**(c)** If $v,w\in T_pM$ are future causal, then $v+w$ is future causal; if
one of $v,w$ is future timelike and the other is future causal, then $v+w$ is
future timelike. Equivalently
$C_p^++\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\subseteq C_p^+$ and
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)+\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)
\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$.

**(a) The underlying manifold.** Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ be Euclidean four-space
as a set and real vector space ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), equipped
with its standard smooth structure, in which the identity map
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is a global smooth chart
([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[prop-open-subsets-of-euclidean-space-have-the-standard-smooth-structure]]).
The coordinate vector fields $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$,
$a=0,1,2,3$, are smooth vector fields on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), and at every
$p\in M$ the tuple
$(\partial_0|_p,\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is a basis of
$T_pM$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(b) The metric.** The **flat metric** $\eta$ is the smooth covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ whose components in the chart $x$ are the constant
functions $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), that is
$$\eta=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2 .$$
It is symmetric, and at every $p$ its matrix in the basis of (a) is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: diagonal, with one negative and three positive
entries and no zero entry. Hence $\eta_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia
$(3,1,0)$, that is, a Lorentz form on $T_pM$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and $(M,\eta)$ is a smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The restriction of $\eta_p$ to
$\operatorname{span}(\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is positive
definite.

**(c) Time orientation.** The field $N:=\partial_0$ satisfies
$\eta(N,N)=-1<0$ pointwise, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,\eta)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). The triple $(M,\eta,N)$ is
the **flat model**. At every $p$ the pointwise vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] applies, and a nonzero causal
$v\in T_pM$ is future-directed exactly when $\eta_p(v,N_p)<0$
([[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]).

**(d) Events, displacements and straight paths.** The points of $M$ are the
**events** of the model. Since $M=\mathbb R^4$ is a vector space, for events
$p,q\in M$ the **displacement** from $p$ to $q$ is the vector $q-p\in M$, and
the **straight path** from $p$ to $q$ is the curve $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ on
$[0,1]$, whose chart representative has the constant velocity $q-p$. For
$v\in\mathbb R^4$ the **translation** is the map $\tau_v(p):=p+v$ of $M$.

**(e) Inertial charts and frames.** A chart of $M$ with domain $M$ is called a
**global chart**. A global chart $y=(y^0,y^1,y^2,y^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is
**inertial** when its components of $\eta$ are the constant functions
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $M$ and its first coordinate vector field
$\partial/\partial y^0$ is future-directed at every point. The chart $x$ of (a)
is inertial: its components of $\eta$ are $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ by
(b), and its first coordinate vector field is $N$, future-directed by (c). If
$y$ is inertial and $o\in M$, the tuple
$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,
\partial/\partial y^2|_o,\partial/\partial y^3|_o)$ is an **inertial frame**
at $o$; its vectors satisfy
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is
future-directed.

**(f) Cone sets.** Let a vector $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ in an inertial chart, write $v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Write
$$C^+:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0>|v_s|\}$$
and $\overline{C^+}:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the coordinate cone
sets. In every inertial chart and at every event $p$,
the future cone $C_p^+$ of (c) consists of exactly those $v$ with
$v^0>|v_s|$, its closure of exactly those with $v^0\ge|v_s|$, and the
future-directed causal vectors of $T_pM$ are exactly the nonzero vectors with
$v^0\ge|v_s|$; moreover the future cone is closed under sums. All of this is
proved in [[lem-gr-flat-inertial-cone-criterion-and-sums]], where the
independence of the inertial chart is also established.

**(g) Scope.** This is a mathematical definition; it asserts nothing about
nature. The physical reading of the flat model is recorded with the framework
postulates of this library and is not part of this definition, and the flat
examples and counterexamples of this page are conditional statements inside
the model.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $f=g$ almost everywhere;
2. for every measurable $A$,
   $$\int_A f\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$

For integrable real or complex $h$, the notation in condition 2 means
$\int_A h\,d\mu:=\int h\chi_A\,d\mu$; the product is integrable because
$|h\chi_A|\le|h|$.

derivations.claim: (Almost-everywhere cone inequality.) Write $c(t):=x(\gamma(t))=(c^0(t),c_s(t))$. By [L1], $c$ is locally absolutely continuous and at almost every $t$ its derivative $c'(t)$ exists and equals the coordinates of the nonzero future causal velocity, so by [L2] $c^0{}'(t)\ge|c_s'(t)|_{\mathrm e}$ and $c^0{}'(t)>0$. This proves nothing yet but fixes the a.e. information used below.

(Monotonicity and the Lipschitz bound.) Let $a<b$ in $I$. By [L3] applied to the absolutely continuous functions $c^0$ and the components of $c_s$ on $[a,b]$, and by [L4], $$c^0(b)-c^0(a)=\int_a^bc^0{}'(t)\,dt\ge\left|\int_a^bc_s'(t)\,dt\right|_{\mathrm e}=|c_s(b)-c_s(a)|_{\mathrm e}\ge0.$$ This is (b). If $c^0(b)=c^0(a)$, then $\int_a^bc^0{}'=0$ with $c^0{}'\ge0$ almost everywhere, so [L4] gives $c^0{}'=0$ almost everywhere on $[a,b]$, contradicting $c^0{}'>0$ on the full-measure set of step 1.1; hence $c^0(b)>c^0(a)$, which is the strict monotonicity of (a). Moreover $c(a)=c(b)$ would give $c_s(a)=c_s(b)$ by the displayed inequality, hence $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, and strict increase of $c^0$ forbids $a<b$; so $\gamma$ is injective, and its spatial coordinates are $1$-Lipschitz in $c^0$ again by the displayed inequality.

(Unboundedness at inextendible ends.) Suppose $\gamma$ is future-inextendible and let $T:=\sup\,(x^0\circ\gamma)(I)$. If $T<+\infty$, then for $t,t'\to\sup I$ the spatial coordinates satisfy $|c_s(t)-c_s(t')|_{\mathrm e}\le|c^0(t)-c^0(t')|\to0$ by step 2.1, so $(c^0,c_s)$ has a limit $q=(T,z_\infty)\in\mathbb R^4$; that is, $\gamma$ converges to the event with coordinates $q$ as $t\to\sup I$. This point limit directly contradicts the no-limit definition of future-inextendibility [L5]. Hence $T=+\infty$; the past statement is the time reverse. With both statements, an inextendible $\gamma$ has range all of $\mathbb R$, and step 2.1 makes $x^0\circ\gamma$ a strictly increasing surjection onto $\mathbb R$, so each level set is attained at exactly one parameter. This proves (c).

(The time coordinate is temporal, and conclusion.) In the coordinates of the global inertial chart, $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and the vector field $w:=-\partial_0$ satisfies $\eta(w,\partial_0)=1$ and $\eta(w,\partial_i)=0$ for $i=1,2,3$; hence $\eta(w,X)=X^0=du(X)$ for every vector $X$, so $w$ is the gradient $\nabla u$ of $u=x^0$. It satisfies $\eta(w,w)=-1<0$ and $du(\partial_0)=1>0$, so $u$ is a temporal function as claimed in (d). With steps 2.1 and 3.1 this completes the proof.

**(a) The underlying manifold.** Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ be Euclidean four-space
as a set and real vector space ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), equipped
with its standard smooth structure, in which the identity map
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is a global smooth chart
([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[prop-open-subsets-of-euclidean-space-have-the-standard-smooth-structure]]).
The coordinate vector fields $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$,
$a=0,1,2,3$, are smooth vector fields on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), and at every
$p\in M$ the tuple
$(\partial_0|_p,\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is a basis of
$T_pM$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(b) The metric.** The **flat metric** $\eta$ is the smooth covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ whose components in the chart $x$ are the constant
functions $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), that is
$$\eta=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2 .$$
It is symmetric, and at every $p$ its matrix in the basis of (a) is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: diagonal, with one negative and three positive
entries and no zero entry. Hence $\eta_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia
$(3,1,0)$, that is, a Lorentz form on $T_pM$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and $(M,\eta)$ is a smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The restriction of $\eta_p$ to
$\operatorname{span}(\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is positive
definite.

**(c) Time orientation.** The field $N:=\partial_0$ satisfies
$\eta(N,N)=-1<0$ pointwise, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,\eta)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). The triple $(M,\eta,N)$ is
the **flat model**. At every $p$ the pointwise vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] applies, and a nonzero causal
$v\in T_pM$ is future-directed exactly when $\eta_p(v,N_p)<0$
([[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]).

**(d) Events, displacements and straight paths.** The points of $M$ are the
**events** of the model. Since $M=\mathbb R^4$ is a vector space, for events
$p,q\in M$ the **displacement** from $p$ to $q$ is the vector $q-p\in M$, and
the **straight path** from $p$ to $q$ is the curve $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ on
$[0,1]$, whose chart representative has the constant velocity $q-p$. For
$v\in\mathbb R^4$ the **translation** is the map $\tau_v(p):=p+v$ of $M$.

**(e) Inertial charts and frames.** A chart of $M$ with domain $M$ is called a
**global chart**. A global chart $y=(y^0,y^1,y^2,y^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is
**inertial** when its components of $\eta$ are the constant functions
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $M$ and its first coordinate vector field
$\partial/\partial y^0$ is future-directed at every point. The chart $x$ of (a)
is inertial: its components of $\eta$ are $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ by
(b), and its first coordinate vector field is $N$, future-directed by (c). If
$y$ is inertial and $o\in M$, the tuple
$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,
\partial/\partial y^2|_o,\partial/\partial y^3|_o)$ is an **inertial frame**
at $o$; its vectors satisfy
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is
future-directed.

**(f) Cone sets.** Let a vector $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ in an inertial chart, write $v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Write
$$C^+:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0>|v_s|\}$$
and $\overline{C^+}:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the coordinate cone
sets. In every inertial chart and at every event $p$,
the future cone $C_p^+$ of (c) consists of exactly those $v$ with
$v^0>|v_s|$, its closure of exactly those with $v^0\ge|v_s|$, and the
future-directed causal vectors of $T_pM$ are exactly the nonzero vectors with
$v^0\ge|v_s|$; moreover the future cone is closed under sums. All of this is
proved in [[lem-gr-flat-inertial-cone-criterion-and-sums]], where the
independence of the inertial chart is also established.

**(g) Scope.** This is a mathematical definition; it asserts nothing about
nature. The physical reading of the flat model is recorded with the framework
postulates of this library and is not part of this definition, and the flat
examples and counterexamples of this page are conditional statements inside
the model.

causal vectors are exactly $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}
=\{v\neq0:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$.

one of $v,w$ is future timelike and the other is future causal, then $v+w$ is
future timelike. Equivalently
$C_p^++\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\subseteq C_p^+$ and
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)+\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)
\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$.
