"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$(U,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ in which every metric component
$g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$ is a constant function on $U$. Then:

**(a)** Every Christoffel symbol of $\nabla$ in the chart vanishes
identically on $U$,
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=0$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b)** The curvature tensor of $\nabla$ vanishes identically on $U$,
$R=0$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]).

**(c)** Every coordinate curve of the chart is a geodesic of $\nabla$; that
is, for fixed constants $c^1,c^2,c^3$ the curve $s\mapsto
x^{-1}(s,c^1,c^2,c^3)$ is a geodesic in the affine parameter $s$
([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]) carrying the product topology of $n$
copies of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]), and let
$d_2$ be the Euclidean metric. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ **is** the metric topology of $d_2$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]), so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as
   a metric space are one topological space, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).
2. A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset for the product
   topology ([[def-compact-space]]) **if and only if** $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only there; for $n = 0$ the product is a
one-point space and is compact. **No choice principle is used**: the metric
statement it is read off from is proved by bisection
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

derivations.claim: (The slab model.) By [L2] the set $M$ is an open submanifold of $A$ with the restricted chart $x$, and the restricted fields $g=\eta|_M$ and $N=\partial_0|_M$ are smooth; the components of $g$ in the restricted chart are the constants $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $g(N,N)=\eta(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-1<0$, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,g)$ and $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold. Applying [L3] to this chart gives the vanishing of the Christoffel symbols and the curvature of the metric-selected connection and the geodesic character of coordinate curves. Since $M$ is open in $A$ and $g$ restricts $\eta$, the notions of locally absolutely continuous curve, velocity and pointwise causal character agree for curves in $M$ whether read in $(M,g)$ or in $(A,\eta)$. This proves (a).

(Monotonicity and Lipschitz bounds.) Let $u:I\to M$ be a future causal curve of $(M,g)$. By (a) it is a future causal curve of $(A,\eta)$, so [L4] applies: $x^0\circ u$ is strictly increasing and $|z(u(t'))-z(u(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le x^0(u(t'))-x^0(u(t))$ for $t<t'$ in $I$, and $x^0\circ u$ is locally absolutely continuous. This is the quantitative input used below.

(Cone characterization and convexity in the slab.) By [L1] and $g=\eta|_M$, the future cones at points of $M$ are those of the chart. Since $M$ is convex in the coordinates of $x$, the straight segment between $p,q\in M$ lies in $M$; if $q-p\in C^+$ (respectively $\overline{C^+}$) the straight path $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ is a future timelike (respectively causal) curve in $M$ from $p$ to $q$, so $q\in I^+_M(p)$ (respectively $q\in J^+_M(p)$). Conversely a future causal curve in $M$ is one in $A$, and [L5] gives $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ when $q\in J^+_M(p)$; for $q\in I^+_M(p)$ the strict cone membership is the same statement with $C^+$. Finally, [L6] gives $C^++\overline{C^+}\subseteq C^+$ and $\overline{C^+}+\overline{C^+}\subseteq\overline{C^+}$.

(The vertical geodesic, its maximal domain and inextendibility.) Let $\gamma(s):=x^{-1}(s,z_0)$ for $s\in(0,1)$. Its coordinate path is $y(s)=(s,z_0)$, so $\dot y=(1,0,0,0)$ and $\ddot y=0$; by [L3] and [L8] it is a smooth geodesic with affine parameter $s$, and its tangent $\gamma'(s)=\partial_0$ satisfies $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-1<0$, so $\gamma$ is a future timelike curve. Suppose a geodesic $\tilde\gamma:(a,b)\to M$ with $a<1/2<b$ restricts to $\gamma$ on $(0,1)$ and has $b>1$. In the chart, both coordinate paths satisfy the first-order geodesic system of [L8] with the same initial data at $s=1/2$, namely $(y,\dot y)=((1/2,z_0),(1,0,0,0))$, because the Christoffel symbols vanish; by uniqueness in [L8] the coordinate paths agree on $(a,b)$, so $\tilde\gamma(s)=x^{-1}(s,z_0)$ for $s\in(1/2,b)$. But for $s\in(1,b)$ the point $(s,z_0)$ does not lie in $x(M)=(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$, so $\tilde\gamma$ is not defined there — a contradiction. The same argument at the past end excludes $a<0$. Hence no geodesic with these data extends the parameter interval beyond $(0,1)$. If $\gamma(s)$ converged to a point $q\in M$ as $s\to1$, then continuity of the chart coordinate $x^0$ on $M$ would give $1=\lim_{s\to1}x^0(\gamma(s))=x^0(q)<1$, a contradiction; hence $\gamma$ is future-inextendible in the sense of clause (d) of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and its affine parameter is bounded above by $1$. Thus $(M,g,N)$ admits an inextendible future timelike geodesic with bounded affine domain: it is timelike geodesically incomplete. This proves (b).

(Range of an inextendible causal curve.) Let $u:I\to M$ be an inextendible causal curve (future-inextendible and past-inextendible). Suppose first that $u$ is future-inextendible, and put $T:=\sup\,(x^0\circ u)(I)\le1$, finite because $x^0<1$ on $M$. If $T<1$, then $x^0\circ u$ is increasing with limit $T$, and by the Lipschitz bound of step 2.1 the spatial curve $z\circ u$ is Cauchy as $t\to\sup I$: for $t,t'$ close to $\sup I$ one has $|z(u(t'))-z(u(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le|x^0(u(t'))-x^0(u(t))|\to0$. By [L9] it converges to some $z_\infty\in\mathbb R^3$; hence $u(t)\to q:=x^{-1}(T,z_\infty)$ as $t\to\sup I$, and $q\in M$ because $T<1$ and $T\ge x^0(u(t_0))>0$ for any fixed $t_0\in I$. This point limit contradicts future-inextendibility directly by [L7]. Hence $T=1$. The past argument is the time reverse and gives $\inf\,(x^0\circ u)(I)=0$; so $x^0\circ u$ is a strictly increasing continuous function on the interval $I$ whose image has infimum $0$ and supremum $1$ and contains neither endpoint (all values lie in $(0,1)$). Therefore its image is exactly the interval $(0,1)$, and for every $c\in(0,1)$ there is exactly one $t\in I$ with $x^0(u(t))=c$: existence by surjectivity, uniqueness by strict monotonicity.

(Strong causality.) Let $p\in M$ and let $U\subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood of $p$. Choose $0<\varepsilon<\min\bigl(x^0(p),\,1-x^0(p)\bigr)$ so small that the open set $V:=\{q\in M:p-\varepsilon e_0\ll_M q\ll_M p+\varepsilon e_0\}$ is contained in $U$; this is possible because $V$ shrinks to $\{p\}$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ (in the chart it is an open double cone around $p$ intersected with $M$). By the choice of $\varepsilon$, the points $p\pm\varepsilon e_0$ lie in $M$. Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a future causal curve with $\gamma(a),\gamma(b)\in V$ and let $a<t<b$. Since $\gamma|_{[a,t]}$ and $\gamma|_{[t,b]}$ are future causal curves, step 2.2 gives $\gamma(t)-\gamma(a)\in\overline{C^+}$ and $\gamma(b)-\gamma(t)\in\overline{C^+}$; since $\gamma(a)\in V$, step 2.2 gives $\gamma(a)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)\in C^+$, and by [L6] $\gamma(t)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)=\bigl(\gamma(a)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)\bigr)+\bigl(\gamma(t)-\gamma(a)\bigr)\in C^+$. Similarly $(p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(b)\in C^+$ and $(p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(t)=\bigl((p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(b)\bigr)+\bigl(\gamma(b)-\gamma(t)\bigr)\in C^+$. By the convexity and cone characterization of step 2.2, $p-\varepsilon e_0\ll_M\gamma(t)\ll_M p+\varepsilon e_0$, that is $\gamma(t)\in V$. Hence no future causal curve leaves $V$ and later re-enters it, and $(M,g,N)$ is strongly causal.

(Compactness of the causal diamonds.) Let $p,q\in M$. By the cone characterization of step 2.2, $$J^+_M(p)\cap J^-_M(q)=\{r\in M:r-p\in\overline{C^+},\ q-r\in\overline{C^+}\}.$$ The corresponding set $K:=\{r\in\mathbb R^4:r-p\in\overline{C^+},\ q-r\in\overline{C^+}\}$ in the chart is closed (the cone is closed) and bounded with $x^0(r)\in[x^0(p),x^0(q)]\subset(0,1)$; hence $K$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb R^4$ by [L9] and, being contained in the open box $x(M)$, it is a compact subset of $x(M)\cong M$. Therefore the diamond $x^{-1}(K)=J^+_M(p)\cap J^-_M(q)$ is compact in $M$.

(The Cauchy slice.) The set $\Sigma_{1/2}=x^{-1}(\{1/2\}\times\mathbb R^3)$ is the level set of the chart coordinate $x^0$ at a regular value, hence an embedded three-dimensional submanifold with a slice chart given by $x$; its tangent space is spanned by $\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3$ with $g(\partial_i,\partial_j)=\delta_{ij}>0$, so it is spacelike. By step 3.1 every inextendible causal curve of $(M,g)$ has $x^0$-range exactly $(0,1)$ and meets the level $x^0=1/2$ in exactly one parameter value; by clause (c) of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] this says that $\Sigma_{1/2}$ is a Cauchy set, and with the first part a Cauchy hypersurface. This proves (c).

(Conclusion.) Part (a) is step 1.1, part (b) is step 2.3, part (c) is step 4.1. By steps 3.2 and 3.3 the model is strongly causal and all its causal diamonds are compact, which is global hyperbolicity in the sense of clause (c) of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]; this is (d). The same model is timelike geodesically incomplete by (b), so in this class global hyperbolicity does not imply geodesic completeness.

risk_review.notes: Read all nine steps and twenty direct suppliers. Global restricted chart forces genuine local AC even under weak Definition. Vertical y(s)=(s,z0) has Γ=0, is maximal on (0,1) and has no point limit in slab at s=1. Lipschitz spatial graph plus completeness forces time range (0,1) for inextendible future curves, giving Cauchy slice. But step 3.3 reverses the current causal-past formula. For p=q=(1/2,0), the actual diamond contains r_n=(1−1/n,0), n≥3; its only ambient limit is absent boundary (1,0), so no subsequence converges in slab and it is noncompact. Owner must correct causal past and review external consumers before closure. No curvature blow-up or singularity conclusion is warranted.

citations.quote:
An **affine connection** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a connection on the tangent bundle $TM$ in the sense of [[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]. Thus it assigns a vector field $
abla_XY$ to two vector fields and is function-linear in the differentiating direction $X$, real-linear in $Y$, and obeys $
abla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f
abla_XY$.

The word affine imposes neither a metric nor torsion freeness. The tangent-bundle specialization allows the Lie bracket of $X,Y$ to be compared with their covariant derivatives; there is no corresponding bracket on sections of a general vector bundle. Manifolds with boundary are allowed, and tangent vectors at their boundary need not be tangent to the boundary. The empty and zero-dimensional manifolds have the unique tangent-bundle connection.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on
$M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) and let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, with Christoffel symbols $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a
\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]])
and metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$. Then:

1. $\nabla$ is torsion-free ([[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]])
   if and only if $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$ for all $a,b,c$ in every
   smooth chart.
2. $\nabla$ is $g$-compatible ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) if and
   only if, in every smooth chart,

$$\partial_ag_{bc}=\sum_{d=0}^{3}\bigl(\Gamma^d{}_{ab}g_{dc}+\Gamma^d{}_{ac}g_{bd}\bigr) \qquad(a,b,c=0,1,2,3).$$

Thus $\nabla$ is metric-selected for $(M,g)$ if and only if both displayed
conditions hold in every smooth chart.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

derivations.claim:
(The zero-coefficient connection.) On the open submanifold $U$, consider the coordinate connection $
abla^{\mathrm c}$ whose Christoffel symbols in $(U,x)$ are all zero; this is an affine connection on $U$ by [L1]. Its coefficients satisfy $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=0=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$, so it is torsion-free; and the compatibility identity of [L2] holds because both sides vanish: the left side is $\partial_ag_{bc}=0$ since the metric components are constant, and the right side is a sum of terms each containing a Christoffel symbol. Hence $
abla^{\mathrm c}$ is a torsion-free metric-compatible connection for the restricted metric $g|_U$; by uniqueness in [L2] it equals the metric-selected connection of $(U,g|_U)$, which is the restriction $
abla|_U$ of the metric-selected connection of $M$ (its restriction is torsion-free and metric-compatible on $U$). Therefore every Christoffel symbol of $
abla$ in $(U,x)$ vanishes on $U$, which is (a).

(The curvature.) Substituting the vanishing coefficients of step 1.1 into the coordinate formula [L3] makes every term vanish identically on $U$, so $R^a{}_{bcd}=0$ on $U$ for all indices; since the curvature is a tensor field, $R=0$ on $U$. This is (b).

(Coordinate curves.) Let $y(s)=(s,c^1,c^2,c^3)$ be the coordinate path of a coordinate curve; then $\dot y=(1,0,0,0)$ and $\ddot y=0$. The right side of the geodesic equation of [L4] vanishes because every $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ vanishes by step 1.1, so the equation holds and the coordinate curve is a geodesic in the affine parameter $s$. This proves (c) and completes the proof.

citations.quote:
Let $M^m$ be a smooth manifold, let $k\in\mathbb N$ satisfy $0\le k\le m$,
and let $S\subseteq M$. One says that $S$ is an **embedded $k$-dimensional
submanifold** of $M$ when for every $p\in S$ there
is a smooth chart $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with $p\in U$
such that

$$\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^k\times\{0\}).$$

Such a chart is a **slice chart** for $S$ at $p$. The topology on $S$ is the
subspace topology inherited from $M$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

The next lemma proves that the restricted slice charts define a smooth
$k$-manifold structure on $S$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$g_p^{-1}$ and $g^{ab}$ be the inverse metric and its chart components as in
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]. Then:

1. For every smooth chart $(U,x)$ the component functions $g^{ab}:U\to\mathbb R$
   are $C^\infty$ on $U$.
2. For overlapping smooth charts $(U,x)$, $(V,y)$ the components satisfy the
   contravariant transformation law

$$g'^{ab}(u)=\sum_{c,d=0}^{3}\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^c}\bigl(x(u)\bigr)\, \frac{\partial y^b}{\partial x^d}\bigl(x(u)\bigr)\,g^{cd}\bigl(x(u)\bigr),\qquad u\in y(U\cap V),$$

where every component evaluated at a coordinate tuple is its coordinate
representative, as in [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
$x(u)$ denotes $(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$, and $\partial y^a/\partial x^c$ are
the entries of $D(y\circ x^{-1})$.

3. Consequently the pointwise bilinear forms $g_p^{-1}$ on $T_p^*M$ are
   presented by component functions that are smooth in every chart and glue by
   the contravariant law; the inverse metric is a well-defined smooth component
   family determined by $g$ alone.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

For a given connection on $E$ and a smooth curve on an interval with nonempty interior, the **covariant derivative along the curve** is
$$D_tV=(\gamma^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial t}V.$$
Here $V$ is a section of the pullback bundle as in [[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]], and the pullback connection exists by [[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. It is real-linear and satisfies $D_t(fV)=f'V+fD_tV$ for functions of the parameter.

At an included endpoint the smooth up-to-boundary coefficients have their one-sided derivative; equivalently any smooth local extension of the coefficients gives this value, because extensions agreeing on a one-sided interval have the same derivative there. For a piecewise smooth curve the derivative is defined on each piece, with separate one-sided derivatives at corners; those derivatives are not required to agree. A singleton interval carries no derivative operator under this convention and will have identity transport by definition. A zero section or a rank-zero bundle gives zero covariant derivative. Constant base curves can have sections with nonzero coefficient derivative.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $M^m$ be a smooth manifold, let $k\in\mathbb N$ satisfy $0\le k\le m$,
and let $S\subseteq M$. One says that $S$ is an **embedded $k$-dimensional
submanifold** of $M$ when for every $p\in S$ there
is a smooth chart $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with $p\in U$
such that

$$\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^k\times\{0\}).$$

Such a chart is a **slice chart** for $S$ at $p$. The topology on $S$ is the
subspace topology inherited from $M$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

The next lemma proves that the restricted slice charts define a smooth
$k$-manifold structure on $S$.

derivations.claim: (A smooth nonzero normal field on a slice chart.) Fix $p\in\Sigma$ and a slice chart $(U,y)$ as in [L1], and put $f:=y^4$, so that $\Sigma\cap U=\{f=0\}$ and $df_q\neq0$ for $q\in\Sigma\cap U$; let $\xi:=\sharp\,df$ on $U$ be the metric dual field of [L2]. Then $\xi$ is smooth on $U$ and nonzero there, and for $q\in\Sigma\cap U$ and $X\in T_q\Sigma$ one has $g_q(\xi_q,X)=df_q(X)=0$ because $X$ is tangent to the level set $\{f=0\}$; hence $\xi_q\in T_q\Sigma^{\perp}\setminus\{0\}$.

(The normal line is one-dimensional and negative definite.) Let $q\in\Sigma$. If $v\in T_q\Sigma\cap T_q\Sigma^{\perp}$, then $g_q(v,v)=0$ because $v$ is orthogonal to itself, while positive definiteness of $g_q|_{T_q\Sigma}$ forces $v=0$; hence $T_q\Sigma\cap T_q\Sigma^{\perp}=\{0\}$. Therefore the quotient map $T_qM\to T_qM/T_q\Sigma$ restricts injectively on $T_q\Sigma^{\perp}$, so $\dim T_q\Sigma^{\perp}\le\dim(T_qM/T_q\Sigma)=1$, and $\xi_q\neq0$ from step 1.1 shows that the dimension is exactly one and that $\dim(T_q\Sigma+T_q\Sigma^{\perp})=4$, that is $T_qM=T_q\Sigma\oplus T_q\Sigma^{\perp}$. If $u\in T_q\Sigma^{\perp}$ is nonzero and $g_q(u,u)\ge0$, then on the direct sum $T_q\Sigma\oplus\mathbb Ru=T_qM$ the form $g_q$ is a block sum of a positive definite form and the form $g_q(u,u)\ge0$ on the line $\mathbb Ru$, hence positive semidefinite with the only possible zero values on $\mathbb Ru$; this contradicts the existence of the timelike time-orientation vector $N_q$ with $g_q(N_q,N_q)<0$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Hence $g_q(u,u)<0$ for every nonzero $u\in T_q\Sigma^{\perp}$: the normal line is negative definite, and in particular nondegenerate.

(Existence and uniqueness of the future unit normal.) Let $q\in\Sigma$. The vector $\xi_q$ is nonzero and, by step 2.1, timelike; so is $N_q$. By [L3] two timelike vectors at $q$ are never orthogonal, so $g_q(\xi_q,N_q)\neq0$, and $$n_q:=-\frac{\operatorname{sign}\bigl(g_q(\xi_q,N_q)\bigr)}{\sqrt{-g_q(\xi_q,\xi_q)}}\,\xi_q$$ is a well-defined element of $T_q\Sigma^{\perp}$ with $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$ and $g_q(n_q,N_q)=-|g_q(\xi_q,N_q)|/\sqrt{-g_q(\xi_q,\xi_q)}<0$. If $m\in T_q\Sigma^{\perp}$ satisfies $g_q(m,m)=-1$ and $g_q(m,N_q)<0$, then $m=t\xi_q$ for some $t\in\mathbb R$ because the line is spanned by $\xi_q$; $g_q(m,m)=t^2g_q(\xi_q,\xi_q)=-1$ gives $t=\pm1/\sqrt{-g_q(\xi_q,\xi_q)}$, and the sign of $g_q(m,N_q)=t\,g_q(\xi_q,N_q)$ is the product of the signs of $t$ and $g_q(\xi_q,N_q)$; the condition $g_q(m,N_q)<0$ therefore selects exactly $t=-\operatorname{sign}(g_q(\xi_q,N_q))/\sqrt{-g_q(\xi_q,\xi_q)}$, that is $m=n_q$. This proves (a).

(Smoothness of the normal along $\Sigma$.) On the slice chart $(U,y)$ of step 1.1, the functions $q\mapsto g_q(\xi_q,\xi_q)$ and $q\mapsto g_q(\xi_q,N_q)$ are smooth on $U$; on $\Sigma\cap U$ the first is negative and the second nonzero by steps 2.1 and 3.1. Shrinking $U$ to a smaller connected neighborhood of a given point of $\Sigma$, we may suppose $g(\xi,\xi)<0$ on all of $U$ and, on the connected set $\Sigma\cap U$, $\operatorname{sign}(g(\xi,N))$ constant; then the formula of step 3.1 defines a smooth ambient field $	ilde n:=-\operatorname{sign}(g(\xi,N))\xi/\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}$ on $U$ whose restriction to $\Sigma\cap U$ is $n$. Such local extensions cover $\Sigma$ and agree on overlaps because all restrict to $n$ on $\Sigma$. Independence of the extensions: let $	ilde n_1,	ilde n_2$ be local extensions of $n$ near $p$ and let $	ilde X$ be a smooth extension of a tangent field with $	ilde X_p=V$; choose a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $\Sigma$ with $\gamma(0)=p$ and $\gamma'(0)=V$. Then $	ilde n_1\circ\gamma=	ilde n_2\circ\gamma$ as curves in $TM$, so by [L4] $
abla_{	ilde X}	ilde n_1|_p=
abla_{	ilde X}	ilde n_2|_p$. For a fixed extension $	ilde n$, the map $X\mapsto
abla_X	ilde n|_p$ is additive and $C^\infty(M)$-linear by the affine-connection laws ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), so its value depends only on $X_p$; hence $
abla_Vn:=
abla_{	ilde X}	ilde n|_p$ is independent of both extensions and is additive in $V$. This proves (b).

($h$ and $K$ are smooth tensor fields.) On $\Sigma\cap U$ of a slice chart, the components $h_{ij}=g_{ij}|_{\Sigma\cap U}$ ($i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$) are smooth functions of the slice coordinates and the matrix $(h_{ij})$ is positive definite by [L1]; since $\Sigma$ is covered by such charts and the local expressions agree on overlaps (both are restrictions of the smooth field $g$), $h$ is a smooth symmetric positive definite covariant $2$-tensor field on $\Sigma$, that is, a Riemannian metric. For $K$, fix $p\in\Sigma$ and choose a local smooth extension $	ilde n$ of $n$ and smooth tangent extensions $	ilde X,	ilde Y$ of fields with $	ilde X_p=V$, $	ilde Y_p=W$; by step 4.1 the number $g_p(
abla_Vn,W):=g_p(
abla_{	ilde X}	ilde n,	ilde Y)$ does not depend on the three extensions. It is additive and $\mathbb R$-bilinear in $(V,W)$ because $
abla$ and $g$ are, and it is $C^\infty(\Sigma)$-linear in each slot: replacing $	ilde X$ by $\varphi	ilde X$ for a smooth function $\varphi$ on $\Sigma$ extended locally changes $
abla_{	ilde X}	ilde n$ by a factor $\varphi$ by the connection law $
abla_{\varphi	ilde X}	ilde n=\varphi
abla_{	ilde X}	ilde n$, and replacing $	ilde Y$ by $\varphi	ilde Y$ multiplies $g(
abla_{	ilde X}	ilde n,	ilde Y)$ by $\varphi$ by bilinearity of $g$; the chart components of $K$ in slice coordinates, $K_{ij}=g(
abla_{\partial_i}	ilde n,\partial_j)$, are then smooth in the slice coordinates because the connection coefficients and $	ilde n$ are smooth. Hence $K$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $\Sigma$.

(Symmetry and the Gauss relation.) Fix $p\in\Sigma$ and $V,W\in T_p\Sigma$; extend $V,W$ to smooth ambient fields $X,Y$ tangent to $\Sigma$ along $\Sigma$, and extend $n$ to a smooth ambient field $	ilde n$ near $p$ (step 4.1). The function $g(	ilde n,Y)$ vanishes identically on $\Sigma$ because $Y$ is tangent and $	ilde n$ normal there; differentiating it along $V$ at $p$ and using [L5] gives $0=g(
abla_V	ilde n,Y)+g(n,
abla_VY)$ at $p$, that is $K_p(V,W)=-g_p(
abla_VW,n_p)$; the same argument with $V$ and $W$ exchanged gives $K_p(W,V)=-g_p(
abla_WV,n_p)$. By torsion-freedom in [L5], $
abla_VW-
abla_WV=[X,Y]$ at $p$, and $[X,Y]$ is tangent to $\Sigma$ at $p$ by [L6]; since $n_p$ is normal, $g_p([X,Y],n_p)=0$. Therefore $K_p(V,W)-K_p(W,V)=-g_p([X,Y],n_p)=0$, so $K$ is symmetric and the displayed Gauss relation holds.

(The shape operator.) Fix $p\in\Sigma$. Since $h_p$ is a positive definite symmetric form on the three-dimensional space $T_p\Sigma$, there is an $h_p$-orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_p\Sigma$ ([[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]); define $S_pV:=\sum_{i=1}^3K_p(V,e_i)\,e_i$ for $V\in T_p\Sigma$. Then $h_p(S_pV,e_j)=K_p(V,e_j)$ for each $j$, and since $\{e_j\}$ is a basis the identity $h_p(S_pV,W)=K_p(V,W)$ holds for all $W\in T_p\Sigma$; this also shows that $S_pV$ does not depend on the chosen orthonormal basis. The assignment $V\mapsto S_pV$ is linear because $K_p$ is bilinear. Self-adjointness is immediate from symmetry of $K$ and of $h_p$: $h_p(S_pV,W)=K_p(V,W)=K_p(W,V)=h_p(S_pW,V)=h_p(V,S_pW)$. Finally, $
abla_Vn\in T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(
abla_Vn,n_p)=	frac12V(g(	ilde n,	ilde n))=0$ because $g(	ilde n,	ilde n)\equiv-1$ on $\Sigma$ and $V$ is tangent, so $
abla_Vn\in n_p^{\perp}$; by [L3] $n_p^{\perp}$ is three-dimensional, and it contains $T_p\Sigma$, also three-dimensional, so $n_p^{\perp}=T_p\Sigma$ and $
abla_Vn\in T_p\Sigma$. For every $W\in T_p\Sigma$ one has $g_p(
abla_Vn,W)=K_p(V,W)=h_p(S_pV,W)$; since $h_p$ is nondegenerate, $
abla_Vn=S_pV$. This proves (d) and completes the proof.
