citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and Einstein tensor $G$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let
$\Sigma\subseteq M$ be a spacelike embedded hypersurface
([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]],
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (a)), and fix real
constants $\kappa$ and $\Lambda$ (the framework coupling constants, purely
parameters for this definition).

**(a) The geometric data.**
For $p\in\Sigma$ the orthogonal complement $T_p\Sigma^{\perp}$ is
one-dimensional and nondegenerate
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]); there is therefore a unique
$n_p\in T_p\Sigma^{\perp}$ with $g_p(n_p,n_p)=-1$ and $g_p(n_p,N_p)<0$ and it
depends smoothly on $p$, the **future unit normal field** of $\Sigma$; this
and the properties of $h$ and $K$ below are proved, not assumed, in
[[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]. Define
on $\Sigma$ the **induced metric** $h$ and the **second fundamental form**
$K$ by
$$h_p(V,W):=g_p(V,W),\qquad K_p(V,W):=g_p(\nabla_Vn,W)\qquad(V,W\in T_p\Sigma),$$
where $\nabla_Vn$ is the covariant derivative at $p$ of the ambient field $n$
in the tangential direction $V$; $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric on
$\Sigma$ and $K$ a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $\Sigma$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]).

**(b) Matter data and constraints.** Let $T$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ (the stress-energy field of a matter branch). Its
**matter data on $\Sigma$** are the smooth fields
$$\rho:=T(n,n),\qquad j(V):=-T(n,V)\quad(V\in T\Sigma).$$
The tuple $(\Sigma,h,K,\rho,j)$ **satisfies the constraint equations** for
$(\kappa,\Lambda)$ when
$$G(n,n)-\Lambda=\kappa\,\rho,\qquad G(n,V)=\kappa\,T(n,V)\quad\text{for every }V\in T_p\Sigma,\ p\in\Sigma .$$
The first is the normal projection of the equation $G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$
evaluated on $(n,n)$, namely $G(n,n)+\Lambda g(n,n)=\kappa T(n,n)$, with
$g(n,n)=-1$; the second is the normal-tangential projection, the term in
$\Lambda$ dropping because $g(n,V)=0$. That a solution of the field equation
satisfies these two projections is proved in
[[lem-gr-constraint-projections]]. The purely tangential projection
$G(V,W)+\Lambda h(V,W)=\kappa T(V,W)$ is not part of the constraints and is
not required here.

**(c) Developments.** A **development** of the data
$(\Sigma,h,K,\rho,j)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
$(M',g',N')$ together with a smooth embedding $\varphi:\Sigma\to M'$ whose
image is a spacelike embedded hypersurface with induced metric $\varphi^*g'=h$
and second fundamental form $K$ with respect to its future unit normal $n'$.
Write $T'$ for the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field included as
the development's stress-energy field. The matter-data matching condition is
the pair of normal projections
$$\rho(p)=T'_{\varphi(p)}(n'_{\varphi(p)},n'_{\varphi(p)}),\qquad j_p(V)=-T'_{\varphi(p)}(n'_{\varphi(p)},d\varphi_p(V))\quad(p\in\Sigma,\ V\in T_p\Sigma).$$
Equivalently, the scalar field $T'(n',n')$ along $\varphi(\Sigma)$ pulls
back to $\rho$, and the covector field $-T'(n',\cdot)$ restricted to
$T\varphi(\Sigma)$ pulls back to $j$. This tuple prescribes only these
stress-energy projections; any additional matter-field data are not included
in $(\Sigma,h,K,\rho,j)$. The development is a **globally hyperbolic
development** when
$\varphi(\Sigma)$ is a Cauchy hypersurface of $(M',g',N')$, so that
$(M',g',N')$ is globally hyperbolic
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]],
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c)).

**(d) Maximality.** A globally hyperbolic development $(M_*,g_*,N_*;
\varphi_*)$ is **maximal** for the data when for every globally hyperbolic
development $(M',g',N';\varphi')$ there is a smooth isometric embedding
$\psi:M'\to M_*$ with $\psi\circ\varphi'=\varphi_*$, $\psi$ preserving the
time orientations and carrying the selected stress-energy tensor $T'$ to
$T_*$, that is, $\psi^*T_*=T'$. Thus maximality is uniqueness up to
data-fixing isometry among globally hyperbolic developments with their selected
stress-energy tensors.

**(e) Scope.** The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of
developments, and it does not assert that $T'$ is generated by matter fields
solving any equation: those claims require the local and global existence theory of
the Einstein-matter system and are not made on this page. The constraint
equations are displayed only as equations satisfied or not by given data.
The equivalent formulation of the constraints in terms of the induced scalar
curvature of $h$ and the divergence of $K$, and the existence theory for
solutions of the constraints, rest on the Gauss-Codazzi relations and on PDE
theory and are deferred to the later pages of this track; no such
equivalence is asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\Sigma\subseteq M$ be a
spacelike embedded hypersurface in the sense of
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (a), so that
$\Sigma$ is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) and the restriction of $g_p$
to $T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for every $p\in\Sigma$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). In the notation of
[[def-gr-spacelike-initial-data-and-constraints]] clause (a), whose claims
this lemma establishes:

**(a) The future unit normal.** For every $p\in\Sigma$ the orthogonal
complement $T_p\Sigma^{\perp}$ is one-dimensional, nondegenerate for $g_p$,
and negative definite: every nonzero $u\in T_p\Sigma^{\perp}$ is timelike,
$g_p(u,u)<0$. Hence there is exactly one $n_p\in T_p\Sigma^{\perp}$ with
$g_p(n_p,n_p)=-1$ and $g_p(n_p,N_p)<0$.

**(b) Smoothness along the hypersurface.** The assignment $p\mapsto n_p$ is
smooth along $\Sigma$: for every $p\in\Sigma$ there are an open neighborhood
$O$ of $p$ in $M$ and a smooth vector field $\tilde n$ on $O$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) with
$\tilde n|_{\Sigma\cap O}=n|_{\Sigma\cap O}$, and for any two such local
extensions the covariant derivative at a point of $\Sigma$ in a direction
tangent to $\Sigma$ agrees. Thus for $V\in T_p\Sigma$ the vector
$\nabla_Vn\in T_pM$ is well defined as $\nabla_{\tilde X}\tilde n|_p$ for any
smooth extensions $\tilde n$ of $n$ and $\tilde X$ of a tangent field with
$\tilde X_p=V$ ([[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]).

**(c) The induced metric and second fundamental form.** The **induced
metric** $h_p(V,W):=g_p(V,W)$ is a smooth Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, and
$$K_p(V,W):=g_p(\nabla_Vn,W)\qquad(V,W\in T_p\Sigma)$$
(the **second fundamental form**) defines a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $K$ on $\Sigma$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) with
$$K_p(V,W)=-g_p(\nabla_VW,n_p),$$
where $\nabla_VW$ is the ambient covariant derivative at $p$ of any smooth
extension of a tangent field with value $W$ at $p$, in the direction of any
extension with value $V$ at $p$.

**(d) The shape operator.** The endomorphism $S_p:T_p\Sigma\to T_p\Sigma$
defined by $h_p(S_pV,W)=K_p(V,W)$ for all $W\in T_p\Sigma$ is well defined,
linear and self-adjoint for the positive definite form $h_p$, and the
Weingarten relation $\nabla_Vn=S_pV$ holds for every $V\in T_p\Sigma$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $M^m$ be a smooth manifold, let $k\in\mathbb N$ satisfy $0\le k\le m$,
and let $S\subseteq M$. One says that $S$ is an **embedded $k$-dimensional
submanifold** of $M$ when for every $p\in S$ there
is a smooth chart $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with $p\in U$
such that

$$\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^k\times\{0\}).$$

Such a chart is a **slice chart** for $S$ at $p$. The topology on $S$ is the
subspace topology inherited from $M$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

The next lemma proves that the restricted slice charts define a smooth
$k$-manifold structure on $S$.

derivations.claim: (Normal projection.) Let $p\in\Sigma$ and evaluate the field equation at $p$ on the pair $(n_p,n_p)$, an evaluation of the smooth covariant $2$-tensor field $G$ of [L1]; by [L4] and [L3], $G(n_p,n_p)+\Lambda\,g_p(n_p,n_p)=\kappa T(n_p,n_p)$. By [L2], $g_p(n_p,n_p)=-1$, and $T(n_p,n_p)=\rho(p)$ by the definition of $\rho$; hence $G(n_p,n_p)-\Lambda=\kappa\rho(p)$.

(Normal-tangential projection.) Let $p\in\Sigma$ and $V\in T_p\Sigma$, and evaluate the field equation at $p$ on the pair $(n_p,V)$; by [L4] and [L3], $G(n_p,V)+\Lambda\,g_p(n_p,V)=\kappa T(n_p,V)$. By [L2], $V$ is tangent to $\Sigma$ and $n_p$ is normal, so $g_p(n_p,V)=0$; hence $G(n_p,V)=\kappa T(n_p,V)=-\kappa\,j(V)$ by the definition of $j$.

(Conclusion for the constraints.) Steps 1.1 and 1.2 give the two displays of clause (a) for arbitrary $p\in\Sigma$ and $V\in T_p\Sigma$, which is exactly the condition defining that $(\Sigma,h,K,\rho,j)$ satisfies the constraint equations in [[def-gr-spacelike-initial-data-and-constraints]] clause (b).

(Smoothness of the matter data.) In a slice chart $(U,y)$ as in [L5], the components $n^a$ of the normal, the components $g_{ab}$ of the metric and the components $T_{ab}$ of the stress-energy field are $C^\infty$ functions of $(y^1,y^2,y^3)$ on $\Sigma\cap U$; hence $\rho=T_{ab}n^an^b$ and $j(V)=-$ the corresponding contraction of $T$ with $n$ and $V$ have $C^\infty$ coordinate expressions in the slice coordinates, for every smooth tangent vector field $V$ on $\Sigma$. Since the slice charts cover $\Sigma$, $\rho$ is a smooth function on $\Sigma$ and $j$ a smooth field on $\Sigma$ (a covariant $1$-tensor field in the sense of the restriction to $\Sigma$ of the formulas above). This is (b) and completes the proof.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps and nine direct suppliers. Under the displayed tensor-equation hypothesis, evaluation at n,n uses g(n,n)=−1; evaluation at n,V uses g(n,V)=0, giving G(n,V)=−κj(V). Smooth local normal extension and smooth T give smooth scalar ρ and covector j. κ=0 and Λ=0 introduce no division; empty hypersurface is vacuous. This is mathematics conditional on a tensor equality, with no claim of empirical field-law truth or converse existence.

boundaries.reason: The level sets, cones and diamonds are nonempty where described; no empty family arises.

No converse is claimed beyond the stated characterisation of V_epsilon(p), which step 2.2 proves directly in both directions.

citations.quote:
**(a) The underlying manifold.** Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ be Euclidean four-space
as a set and real vector space ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), equipped
with its standard smooth structure, in which the identity map
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is a global smooth chart
([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[prop-open-subsets-of-euclidean-space-have-the-standard-smooth-structure]]).
The coordinate vector fields $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$,
$a=0,1,2,3$, are smooth vector fields on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), and at every
$p\in M$ the tuple
$(\partial_0|_p,\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is a basis of
$T_pM$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(b) The metric.** The **flat metric** $\eta$ is the smooth covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ whose components in the chart $x$ are the constant
functions $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), that is
$$\eta=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2 .$$
It is symmetric, and at every $p$ its matrix in the basis of (a) is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: diagonal, with one negative and three positive
entries and no zero entry. Hence $\eta_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia
$(3,1,0)$, that is, a Lorentz form on $T_pM$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and $(M,\eta)$ is a smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The restriction of $\eta_p$ to
$\operatorname{span}(\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is positive
definite.

**(c) Time orientation.** The field $N:=\partial_0$ satisfies
$\eta(N,N)=-1<0$ pointwise, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,\eta)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). The triple $(M,\eta,N)$ is
the **flat model**. At every $p$ the pointwise vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] applies, and a nonzero causal
$v\in T_pM$ is future-directed exactly when $\eta_p(v,N_p)<0$
([[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]).

**(d) Events, displacements and straight paths.** The points of $M$ are the
**events** of the model. Since $M=\mathbb R^4$ is a vector space, for events
$p,q\in M$ the **displacement** from $p$ to $q$ is the vector $q-p\in M$, and
the **straight path** from $p$ to $q$ is the curve $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ on
$[0,1]$, whose chart representative has the constant velocity $q-p$. For
$v\in\mathbb R^4$ the **translation** is the map $\tau_v(p):=p+v$ of $M$.

**(e) Inertial charts and frames.** A chart of $M$ with domain $M$ is called a
**global chart**. A global chart $y=(y^0,y^1,y^2,y^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is
**inertial** when its components of $\eta$ are the constant functions
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $M$ and its first coordinate vector field
$\partial/\partial y^0$ is future-directed at every point. The chart $x$ of (a)
is inertial: its components of $\eta$ are $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ by
(b), and its first coordinate vector field is $N$, future-directed by (c). If
$y$ is inertial and $o\in M$, the tuple
$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,
\partial/\partial y^2|_o,\partial/\partial y^3|_o)$ is an **inertial frame**
at $o$; its vectors satisfy
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is
future-directed.

**(f) Cone sets.** Let a vector $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ in an inertial chart, write $v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Write
$$C^+:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0>|v_s|\}$$
and $\overline{C^+}:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the coordinate cone
sets. In every inertial chart and at every event $p$,
the future cone $C_p^+$ of (c) consists of exactly those $v$ with
$v^0>|v_s|$, its closure of exactly those with $v^0\ge|v_s|$, and the
future-directed causal vectors of $T_pM$ are exactly the nonzero vectors with
$v^0\ge|v_s|$; moreover the future cone is closed under sums. All of this is
proved in [[lem-gr-flat-inertial-cone-criterion-and-sums]], where the
independence of the inertial chart is also established.

**(g) Scope.** This is a mathematical definition; it asserts nothing about
nature. The physical reading of the flat model is recorded with the framework
postulates of this library and is not part of this definition, and the flat
examples and counterexamples of this page are conditional statements inside
the model.

Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], with its global inertial
chart $x=(x^0,z)$, its cone sets $C^+,\overline{C^+}$ of clause (f) and its
translation action of clause (d), and with the causal relations of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** For every $p\in M$, $J^+(p)=p+\overline{C^+}$ and
$I^+(p)=p+C^+$, where the sum is the translation of clause (d), the cone sets
are those of clause (f), and the displacement is read in the vector space
$M=\mathbb R^4$; in the chart,
$$q\in J^+(p)\Longleftrightarrow x^0(q)-x^0(p)\ge|z(q)-z(p)|_{\mathrm e}.$$

**(b)** For every $c\in\mathbb R$ the level set
$\Sigma_c:=x^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a spacelike embedded hypersurface of $M$, and
every inextendible causal curve of $M$ meets $\Sigma_c$ in exactly one
parameter value; equivalently, $\Sigma_c$ is a Cauchy hypersurface in the
sense of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c).

**(c)** For all $p,q\in M$ the causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is
compact.

**(d)** The model is strongly causal in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (b); hence it is
globally hyperbolic in the sense of clause (c) of that definition.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the
flat model of [[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], with its
global inertial chart $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, written $x=(x^0,z)$ with
$z\in\mathbb R^3$ (clauses (a), (b) and (e) of that definition), and let
$\gamma:I\to M$ be a future causal curve in the class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** $x^0\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R$ is strictly increasing.

**(b)** For all $a<b$ in $I$,
$$\bigl|z(\gamma(b))-z(\gamma(a))\bigr|\le x^0(\gamma(b))-x^0(\gamma(a)),$$
and consequently $\gamma$ is injective and its image is a $1$-Lipschitz graph
over the interval $(x^0\circ\gamma)(I)$.

**(c)** If $\gamma$ is future-inextendible then
$\sup\,(x^0\circ\gamma)(I)=+\infty$; if $\gamma$ is past-inextendible then
$\inf\,(x^0\circ\gamma)(I)=-\infty$. Hence if $\gamma$ is inextendible then
$x^0\circ\gamma$ is a strictly increasing surjection onto $\mathbb R$, and
for every $c\in\mathbb R$ the parameter set
$\{t\in I:x^0(\gamma(t))=c\}$ is a singleton.

**(d)** The coordinate function $u:=x^0$ is a temporal function of the flat
model in the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]
clause (e): its gradient is the vector field $\nabla u=-\partial_0$ on all of
$M$, with $\eta(\nabla u,\nabla u)=-1<0$ and $du(\partial_0)=1>0$
everywhere.

Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], with its global inertial
chart $x=(x^0,z)$, its cone sets $C^+,\overline{C^+}$ of clause (f) and its
translation action of clause (d), and with the causal relations of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** For every $p\in M$, $J^+(p)=p+\overline{C^+}$ and
$I^+(p)=p+C^+$, where the sum is the translation of clause (d), the cone sets
are those of clause (f), and the displacement is read in the vector space
$M=\mathbb R^4$; in the chart,
$$q\in J^+(p)\Longleftrightarrow x^0(q)-x^0(p)\ge|z(q)-z(p)|_{\mathrm e}.$$

**(b)** For every $c\in\mathbb R$ the level set
$\Sigma_c:=x^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a spacelike embedded hypersurface of $M$, and
every inextendible causal curve of $M$ meets $\Sigma_c$ in exactly one
parameter value; equivalently, $\Sigma_c$ is a Cauchy hypersurface in the
sense of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c).

**(c)** For all $p,q\in M$ the causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is
compact.

**(d)** The model is strongly causal in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (b); hence it is
globally hyperbolic in the sense of clause (c) of that definition.

Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], let $y$ be an inertial
chart, let $p\in M$, and let $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$v=v^0\partial_0+\dots+v^3\partial_3$ in the chart
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]). Write
$v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and $|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

**(a)** For every nonzero $v\in T_pM$: $v$ is future timelike iff
$v^0>|v_s|$, and past timelike iff $v^0<-|v_s|$; $v$ is future null iff
$0<v^0=|v_s|$, and past null iff $0<-v^0=|v_s|$; $v$ is future causal iff
$v^0\ge|v_s|$, past causal iff $v^0\le-|v_s|$, and causal iff
$|v^0|\ge|v_s|$; and every nonzero future causal $v$ satisfies $v^0>0$.

**(b)** $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)=\{v\in T_pM:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; the future-directed
causal vectors are exactly $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}
=\{v\neq0:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$.

**(c)** If $v,w\in T_pM$ are future causal, then $v+w$ is future causal; if
one of $v,w$ is future timelike and the other is future causal, then $v+w$ is
future timelike. Equivalently
$C_p^++\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\subseteq C_p^+$ and
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)+\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)
\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$.

Let $M^m$ be a smooth manifold, let $k\in\mathbb N$ satisfy $0\le k\le m$,
and let $S\subseteq M$. One says that $S$ is an **embedded $k$-dimensional
submanifold** of $M$ when for every $p\in S$ there
is a smooth chart $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with $p\in U$
such that

$$\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^k\times\{0\}).$$

Such a chart is a **slice chart** for $S$ at $p$. The topology on $S$ is the
subspace topology inherited from $M$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

The next lemma proves that the restricted slice charts define a smooth
$k$-manifold structure on $S$.

**(a) The underlying manifold.** Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ be Euclidean four-space
as a set and real vector space ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), equipped
with its standard smooth structure, in which the identity map
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is a global smooth chart
([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[prop-open-subsets-of-euclidean-space-have-the-standard-smooth-structure]]).
The coordinate vector fields $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$,
$a=0,1,2,3$, are smooth vector fields on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), and at every
$p\in M$ the tuple
$(\partial_0|_p,\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is a basis of
$T_pM$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(b) The metric.** The **flat metric** $\eta$ is the smooth covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ whose components in the chart $x$ are the constant
functions $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), that is
$$\eta=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2 .$$
It is symmetric, and at every $p$ its matrix in the basis of (a) is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: diagonal, with one negative and three positive
entries and no zero entry. Hence $\eta_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia
$(3,1,0)$, that is, a Lorentz form on $T_pM$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and $(M,\eta)$ is a smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The restriction of $\eta_p$ to
$\operatorname{span}(\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is positive
definite.

**(c) Time orientation.** The field $N:=\partial_0$ satisfies
$\eta(N,N)=-1<0$ pointwise, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,\eta)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). The triple $(M,\eta,N)$ is
the **flat model**. At every $p$ the pointwise vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] applies, and a nonzero causal
$v\in T_pM$ is future-directed exactly when $\eta_p(v,N_p)<0$
([[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]).

**(d) Events, displacements and straight paths.** The points of $M$ are the
**events** of the model. Since $M=\mathbb R^4$ is a vector space, for events
$p,q\in M$ the **displacement** from $p$ to $q$ is the vector $q-p\in M$, and
the **straight path** from $p$ to $q$ is the curve $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ on
$[0,1]$, whose chart representative has the constant velocity $q-p$. For
$v\in\mathbb R^4$ the **translation** is the map $\tau_v(p):=p+v$ of $M$.

**(e) Inertial charts and frames.** A chart of $M$ with domain $M$ is called a
**global chart**. A global chart $y=(y^0,y^1,y^2,y^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is
**inertial** when its components of $\eta$ are the constant functions
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $M$ and its first coordinate vector field
$\partial/\partial y^0$ is future-directed at every point. The chart $x$ of (a)
is inertial: its components of $\eta$ are $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ by
(b), and its first coordinate vector field is $N$, future-directed by (c). If
$y$ is inertial and $o\in M$, the tuple
$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,
\partial/\partial y^2|_o,\partial/\partial y^3|_o)$ is an **inertial frame**
at $o$; its vectors satisfy
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is
future-directed.

**(f) Cone sets.** Let a vector $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ in an inertial chart, write $v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Write
$$C^+:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0>|v_s|\}$$
and $\overline{C^+}:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the coordinate cone
sets. In every inertial chart and at every event $p$,
the future cone $C_p^+$ of (c) consists of exactly those $v$ with
$v^0>|v_s|$, its closure of exactly those with $v^0\ge|v_s|$, and the
future-directed causal vectors of $T_pM$ are exactly the nonzero vectors with
$v^0\ge|v_s|$; moreover the future cone is closed under sums. All of this is
proved in [[lem-gr-flat-inertial-cone-criterion-and-sums]], where the
independence of the inertial chart is also established.

**(g) Scope.** This is a mathematical definition; it asserts nothing about
nature. The physical reading of the flat model is recorded with the framework
postulates of this library and is not part of this definition, and the flat
examples and counterexamples of this page are conditional statements inside
the model.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]) carrying the product topology of $n$
copies of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]), and let
$d_2$ be the Euclidean metric. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ **is** the metric topology of $d_2$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]), so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as
   a metric space are one topological space, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).
2. A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset for the product
   topology ([[def-compact-space]]) **if and only if** $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only there; for $n = 0$ the product is a
one-point space and is compact. **No choice principle is used**: the metric
statement it is read off from is proved by bisection
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

derivations.claim: (The level sets.) By [L4] each $\Sigma_c$ is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold with tangent space $\operatorname{span}(\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)$ on which $\eta$ restricts to $\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1)>0$; hence $\Sigma_c$ is a spacelike embedded hypersurface. Its normal line is spanned by $\partial_0$ with $\eta(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-1$, and $g(\partial_0,N)=g(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-1<0$ with $N=\partial_0$, so $\partial_0$ is the future unit normal. This proves (i).

(The coordinate is temporal.) The function $t=x^0$ has differential $dt$ with $dt(\partial_0)=1$ and $dt(\partial_a)=0$ for $a=1,2,3$; the vector field $w:=-\partial_0$ satisfies $\eta(w,X)=dt(X)$ for every $X$ because $\eta(-\partial_0,\partial_0)=\eta(\partial_0,\partial_0)(-1)=1$ and $\eta(-\partial_0,\partial_a)=0$; hence $
abla t=w$ with $\eta(
abla t,
abla t)=-1<0$ and $dt(\partial_0)=1>0$. This is (ii).

(The double cone is causally convex.) Let $p\in A$, $\varepsilon>0$, let $\gamma:[a,b]\to A$ be future causal with $\gamma(a),\gamma(b)\in V_\varepsilon(p)$ and let $a<s<b$. Since $\gamma(a)\in I^+(p-\varepsilon e_0)$, [L1] gives $\gamma(a)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)\in C^+$; since $\gamma|_{[a,s]}$ is future causal, [L1] gives $\gamma(s)-\gamma(a)\in\overline{C^+}$; by [L3], $\gamma(s)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)\in C^+$, so $p-\varepsilon e_0\ll\gamma(s)$. Similarly $\gamma(b)\in I^-(p+\varepsilon e_0)$ gives $(p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(b)\in C^+$; since $\gamma|_{[s,b]}$ is future causal, $\gamma(b)-\gamma(s)\in\overline{C^+}$ and [L3] gives $(p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(s)\in C^+$, so $\gamma(s)\ll p+\varepsilon e_0$. Hence $\gamma(s)\in V_\varepsilon(p)$, which is causally convex. The displayed coordinate description follows from [L1]: $q\in V_\varepsilon(p)$ iff $(x^0(q)-x^0(p)+\varepsilon,\ z(q)-z(p))\in C^+$ and $(x^0(p)+\varepsilon-x^0(q),\ z(p)-z(q))\in C^+$, i.e. $|z(q)-z(p)|_{\mathrm e}<\varepsilon+x^0(q)-x^0(p)$ and $|z(q)-z(p)|_{\mathrm e}<\varepsilon-x^0(q)+x^0(p)$, which is the stated inequality. This proves (iii).

(The diamond is compact.) Let $r\in A$ with coordinates $(t_r,z_r)$. By [L1], $r\in J^+(o)$ means $t_r\ge|z_r|_{\mathrm e}$ and $r\in J^-(Te_0)$ means $T-t_r\ge|z_r|_{\mathrm e}$; this is the displayed description. The set described is closed (non-strict inequalities of continuous functions) and bounded: $t_r\in[0,T]$ and $|z_r|_{\mathrm e}\le\min(t_r,T-t_r)\le T/2$. By [L5] it is compact, and its $t$-section is the closed ball of radius $\min(t,T-t)$ in $\mathbb R^3$. This proves (iv).

(The domain of dependence is everything.) Let $p\in A$ with $t(p)\ge c$, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be any past-inextendible causal curve through $p$. I claim $\inf\,(t\circ\gamma)(I)=-\infty$. Otherwise put $m:=\inf\,(t\circ\gamma)(I)>-\infty$. Since $t\circ\gamma$ is increasing, it tends to $m$ as the parameter tends to $\inf I$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ choose a parameter $a\in I$ with $m\le t(\gamma(a))<m+\varepsilon$. For any $u,v\in I$ with $u,v\le a$, the Lipschitz bound [L2] gives $|z(\gamma(u))-z(\gamma(v))|_{\mathrm e}\le |t(\gamma(u))-t(\gamma(v))|<\varepsilon$. Thus the full spatial tail is Cauchy as the parameter tends to $\inf I$; by completeness [L8] it converges to some $z_\infty\in\mathbb R^3$. Since $t(\gamma(\cdot))\to m$, the full curve tail converges to $x^{-1}(m,z_\infty)\in A$, contradicting past-inextendibility by clause (d) of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Hence its time range is unbounded below. Since $t\circ\gamma$ is continuous and strictly increasing on the interval $I$ and attains $t(p)\ge c$ at the parameter of $p$, its image contains $(-\infty,t(p)]$, in particular $c$; so some parameter lies on $\Sigma_c$ and $p\in D^+(\Sigma_c)$. The case $t(p)\le c$ is the time reverse: every future-inextendible causal curve through $p$ has time range unbounded above and hence meets $\Sigma_c$, so $p\in D^-(\Sigma_c)$. Therefore $D^+(\Sigma_c)\cup D^-(\Sigma_c)=A$, which is (v).

**(a) The underlying manifold.** Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ be Euclidean four-space
as a set and real vector space ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), equipped
with its standard smooth structure, in which the identity map
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is a global smooth chart
([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[prop-open-subsets-of-euclidean-space-have-the-standard-smooth-structure]]).
The coordinate vector fields $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$,
$a=0,1,2,3$, are smooth vector fields on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), and at every
$p\in M$ the tuple
$(\partial_0|_p,\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is a basis of
$T_pM$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(b) The metric.** The **flat metric** $\eta$ is the smooth covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ whose components in the chart $x$ are the constant
functions $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), that is
$$\eta=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2 .$$
It is symmetric, and at every $p$ its matrix in the basis of (a) is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: diagonal, with one negative and three positive
entries and no zero entry. Hence $\eta_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia
$(3,1,0)$, that is, a Lorentz form on $T_pM$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and $(M,\eta)$ is a smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The restriction of $\eta_p$ to
$\operatorname{span}(\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is positive
definite.

**(c) Time orientation.** The field $N:=\partial_0$ satisfies
$\eta(N,N)=-1<0$ pointwise, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,\eta)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). The triple $(M,\eta,N)$ is
the **flat model**. At every $p$ the pointwise vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] applies, and a nonzero causal
$v\in T_pM$ is future-directed exactly when $\eta_p(v,N_p)<0$
([[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]).

**(d) Events, displacements and straight paths.** The points of $M$ are the
**events** of the model. Since $M=\mathbb R^4$ is a vector space, for events
$p,q\in M$ the **displacement** from $p$ to $q$ is the vector $q-p\in M$, and
the **straight path** from $p$ to $q$ is the curve $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ on
$[0,1]$, whose chart representative has the constant velocity $q-p$. For
$v\in\mathbb R^4$ the **translation** is the map $\tau_v(p):=p+v$ of $M$.

**(e) Inertial charts and frames.** A chart of $M$ with domain $M$ is called a
**global chart**. A global chart $y=(y^0,y^1,y^2,y^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is
**inertial** when its components of $\eta$ are the constant functions
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $M$ and its first coordinate vector field
$\partial/\partial y^0$ is future-directed at every point. The chart $x$ of (a)
is inertial: its components of $\eta$ are $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ by
(b), and its first coordinate vector field is $N$, future-directed by (c). If
$y$ is inertial and $o\in M$, the tuple
$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,
\partial/\partial y^2|_o,\partial/\partial y^3|_o)$ is an **inertial frame**
at $o$; its vectors satisfy
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is
future-directed.

**(f) Cone sets.** Let a vector $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ in an inertial chart, write $v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Write
$$C^+:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0>|v_s|\}$$
and $\overline{C^+}:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the coordinate cone
sets. In every inertial chart and at every event $p$,
the future cone $C_p^+$ of (c) consists of exactly those $v$ with
$v^0>|v_s|$, its closure of exactly those with $v^0\ge|v_s|$, and the
future-directed causal vectors of $T_pM$ are exactly the nonzero vectors with
$v^0\ge|v_s|$; moreover the future cone is closed under sums. All of this is
proved in [[lem-gr-flat-inertial-cone-criterion-and-sums]], where the
independence of the inertial chart is also established.

**(g) Scope.** This is a mathematical definition; it asserts nothing about
nature. The physical reading of the flat model is recorded with the framework
postulates of this library and is not part of this definition, and the flat
examples and counterexamples of this page are conditional statements inside
the model.

For the general causal-curve conclusions (c) and (d), assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) as required by the absolutely continuous flat-curve calculus. ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clauses (a) and (c)):

value. Hence $\Sigma_{1/2}$ is a Cauchy hypersurface.

diamonds $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$, $p,q\in M$, are compact; hence it is globally
hyperbolic in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c).

([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let

identically on $U$,
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=0$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b)** The curvature tensor of $\nabla$ vanishes identically on $U$,

[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]).

**(c)** Every coordinate curve of the chart is a geodesic of $\nabla$; that

([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]).

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let

**(a)** Every Christoffel symbol of $\nabla$ in the chart vanishes
identically on $U$,

**(b)** The curvature tensor of $\nabla$ vanishes identically on $U$,

[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]).

**(c)** Every coordinate curve of the chart is a geodesic of $\nabla$; that
is, for fixed constants $c^1,c^2,c^3$ the curve $s\mapsto
x^{-1}(s,c^1,c^2,c^3)$ is a geodesic in the affine parameter $s$
([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the velocity derivation of
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] translated to the parameter
value $t$. In a chart around $\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** A **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

For the general causal-curve conclusions (c) and (d), assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) as required by the absolutely continuous flat-curve calculus. The geometric restriction and explicit incomplete geodesic in (a)-(b) use no choice premise.

$$M:=x^{-1}\bigl((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3\bigr)=\{p\in A:0<x^0(p)<1\},$$
an open subset of $A$, and let $g:=\eta|_M$ and $N:=\partial_0|_M$ be the

([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clauses (a) and (c)):

**(d) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is strongly causal and its causal
